Chapter 1

The Constitutional Development of India

7 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (23 points)

Acts Passed for the British East India

Company Rule (1773-1853)

  • The Regulating Act of 1773 designated the governor of Bengal, Warren Hastings, as the Governor General of Bengal and subsumed the Presidencies of Madras and Bombay under Bengal's control.
  • The Governor General was provided with an executive council of four to assist him in Military and Non - Military decisions which would be made by the majority of the council.
  • Governor General could vote only in case of tie, in other words Governal-General had a casting vote in case of an equal division.
  • A Supreme Court which had a Chief Justice and three other Judges, was established at Fort William in Calcutta in the year 1774 by this Act. This Act prohibited the Servants of the company from engaging in private trade or accepting gifts and bribes from the Indians.
  • The British Government strengthened its control over the company through the Court of Directors (Governing body of The Company) to report on its revenue, civil and military affairs in India.
  • Pitts India Act 1784 distinguished between the commercial and political functions of the company.
  • Board of Control was created for political matters, and the Court of Directors controlled the commercial affairs.
  • Board of Control was comprised of 6 people.
  • Act of 1786 provided that Governor General could overrule his council in matters of importance affecting the safety, peace or interest of the Empire in India.
  • Governor General was granted the powers of Commander-in-Chief.
  • Lord Cornwallis was the first Governor General to enjoy these powers.
  • The Charter Act of 1793 further extended the commercial monopoly of the company for another 20 years.
  • Charter Act of 1813 for the first time, made provision of at least 1 Lakh rupees per year to be spent on the education, revival and improvement of literature, etc. of Indians. It ended the company's monopoly over trade, although the monopoly over trade of tea & trade with China continued.
  • Charter Act of 1833 made the Governor General of Bengal the Governor General of India and vested in him all civil and military powers.
  • Lord William Bentinck became the first Governor General of India.
  • It ended the Activities of East India Company as a commercial body, which became purely an administrative body.
  • A legal member (fourth member) was included in the council (executive) of Governor General.
  • Macaulay was the first legal member. This law member was entitled to act only for legislative purposes.
  • Charter Act of 1853 separated for the first time the legislative and executive functions of the Governor General's council.
  • It established a separate Indian (Central) legislative council for law-making.
  • It introduced an open competition system for the selection and recruitment of Civil Servants.

Regulating Act 1773 → Supreme Court at Fort William, Calcutta; set up in 1774; first Chief Justice Sir Elijah Impey. Must know

UP2 papers question

Regulating Act 1773 → Supreme Court; Pitt's India Act 1784 → Board of Control; Charter Act 1813 → English missionaries allowed; Charter Act 1833 → Law Member in GG's Council.

Memory aid Court → Control → Christians → Codes: the four Acts in time order.

UP1 paper question

English education came from all three: Charter Act 1813 (Rs 1 lakh a year for education), General Committee of Public Instruction 1823, and the Orientalist-Anglicist Controversy.

1 paper question

Charter Act 1813 → ended East India Company's trade monopoly in India, except tea and China trade; Charter Act 1833 ended its commercial role altogether.

Don't confuse 1813 (monopoly ended except tea and China) with 1833 (Company left with political functions only).

UP1 paper question

Charter Act 1813 → Company lost its trade monopoly with India but kept monopoly of trade with China and in tea.

1 paper question

Charter Act 1813: ended trade monopoly (except tea, China) and asserted British Crown sovereignty over Company territories; territory and revenue stayed with Company for 20 more years.

1 paper question

Charter Act 1833, Section 87 → no Indian barred from Company posts for religion, birth, descent or colour; first opening for Indians in administration.

UP1 paper question

Chapter 2

Acts Passed under the British Crown (1858-1947)

27 facts · 4 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (27 points)
  • The British Crown decided to assume sovereignty over India from the East India Company by the Government of India Act 1858.
  • The Governor General also came to be called the 'Viceroy' of India. He became the direct representative of the British Crown.
  • Lord Canning became the first Viceroy of India.
  • The Board of Control and Court of Directors came to an end. A new post that was the Secretary of State of India was created.
  • He was assisted by a council of 15 members. He received the powers so long enjoyed by the Court of Directors and Board of Control.
  • The council of India was to be advisory in nature, in most cases the initiatives and the final decision remained with the Secretary of State for India. Indian Councils Act 1861, initiated the participation of the Indian representatives in law-making process.
  • The Act restored the legislative powers of making and amending laws to the provinces of Madras and Bombay, thus initiating the process of decentralization.
  • The Act empowered the Viceroy to issue ordinances in case of emergency, which were not to remain in force for more than six months. Indian Councils Act 1892, increased the number of non-official members in both the Central and Provincial Legislative councils but maintained the official majority in them.
  • The Indian members were granted the right to ask questions and discuss the budget in the legislative council.
  • This Act introduced the principle of election, in a limited sense, though the word 'election' was very carefully avoided in it. Indian Councils Act 1909 is also known as the Morley-Minto Reforms.
  • It provided (for the first time) for the association of Indians with the executive councils of Viceroy & Governors. Satyendra Prasad (Prasanna) Sinha became the first Indian to join the Viceroy's Executive Council. He was appointed as a law member.
  • The functions and size of legislatures both at the centre and in the provinces were enlarged. The members of council were given the right to discussion and ask Supplementary questions. The Act provided separate electorates for Muslims. Hence Lord Minto came to be known as The father of the communal electorate. Government of India Act 1919 is known by the name of ‘Montague-Chelmsford Reforms.
  • This Act, for the first time, adopted the Direct Election system.
  • Principle of communal representation was extended by providing separate electorates for Sikhs, Indian Christians, Europeans and Anglo - Indians. It introduced Bicameralism at Central level.
  • It separated various subjects, as the Central and provincial subjects. The Bicameral Central Legislature could make laws for the whole of British India.
  • It introduced dyarchy in the provinces.
  • Provincial subjects were further divided into two parts: transferred and reserved. For the first time, the term, responsible Government was used.
  • Under this Act, a commission was to be constituted after 10 years which will review the working of this Act and present its report. In November 1927 (i.e. 2 years before the schedule), the British Government announced the appointment of a seven- member statutory commission under the chairmanship of Simon to report on the condition of India under its new constitution. The commission was hence called the Simon Commission.
  • Government of India Act 1935 provided for the establishment of an All India Federation consisting of provinces and Princely states as units.
  • It provided for dyarchy at the centre (Which never came into existence) and abolished the same in the provinces.
  • It provided for the establishment of a Reserve Bank of India to control the currency and credit of the country.
  • Principle of Communal representation was further extended by providing separate electorates for Scheduled Castes, women and labourers.
  • A Federal Court was set up in 1937 through this Act.
  • This Act separated Burma from the British India and established two new provinces-Sindh and Orissa (now Odisha).
  • It introduced bicameralism in 6 out of 11 provinces. Indian Independence Act of1947 declared India to be an Independent dominion nation on 15 August 1947.
  • It abolished the office of Viceroy and, a Governor General was appointed for each dominion.
  • It dropped the title of 'Emperor of India' from the royal titles of the King of the United Kingdom.

Indian Councils Act 1861 → portfolio system (five members, sixth added 1874); 6 to 12 additional members for legislation; no split of State and Central subjects.

Chapter 3

Constituent Assembly and making of the Constitution

48 facts · 11 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (29 points)
  • The first formal demand for the Constituent Assembly was made by the Swaraj Party at a conference in Ranchi held in May, 1934.
  • The idea of a Constituent Assembly was put forward for the first time by M.N. Roy in the year 1934.
  • The Indian National Congress officially demanded (after the Swaraj Party) a Constituent Assembly to frame the Constitution of India for the first time in May 1934, at Patna.
  • In 1938, Jawahar Lal Nehru, on behalf of the INC, declared that the constitution of free India must be framed, without outside interference, by a constituent Assembly elected on the basis of adult Franchise. The Demand was finally accepted in principle in the August offer of 1940.
  • The Constituent Assembly was constituted under the scheme formulated by the Cabinet Mission Plan 1946.
  • Number of representatives from provinces was based on their population i.e. about One representative per 10 Lakh people. Ofthese, 296 were to be allotted to British India and 93 Seats to the Princely States. Out of296 seats allotted to British India, 292 members were to be drawn from the eleven governor's provinces and four from the four Chief Commissioners' provinces, one from each.
  • The representatives of Princely states were to be nominated by the heads of the Princely states.
  • The elections to the constituent assembly for 296 seats were held in July-August 1946. The Indian National Congress won 208 seats, the Muslim League won 73 seats, and the small groups and independents got the remaining 15 seats.
  • In the beginning, Princely states did not participate in the Constituent Assembly, but with the third session of the Constituent Assembly commencing on 28 April, 1947 the representatives of the Princely States of India began to join it gradually.
  • Constituent Assembly was a result of an Indirect election.
  • This election was not based on the Adult franchise.
  • According to Government of India Act 1935, voting rights were limited and based on tax, education and property.
  • The Viceroy invited the elected representatives for the first meeting of Constituent Assembly on 9 December 1946.
  • 207 members participated in the first meeting. The meeting was presided over by Dr. Sachchidanand Sinha, the temporary President. Later, on 11 December 1946, Dr. Rajendra Prasad was unanimously elected as the President of the Constituent Assembly. It took 2 years, 11 months and 17 days (according to the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha website) to complete the task of Constitution making.
  • A Total of 11 Sessions (165 days) were held.
  • On 26 November 1949, i.e. the last day of 11th session, the Constitution was adopted. Except for these 11 sessions the constituent assembly finally met on 24 January 1950 to get the signatures of the members on the constitution.
  • Benegal Narsing Rau (B.N. Rau) was appointed as the constitutional advisor to the assembly.
  • On 26 November 1949, the people of India adopted, enacted and gave to themselves the constitution of India.
  • Some provisions of the constitution came into force on 26 November 1949 itself but it completely came into force on 26 January 1950.
  • The number of women in the constituent assembly was 15.
  • They were 1- Vijayalakshmi Pandit, 2- Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, 3- Sarojini Naidu, 4- Sucheta Kripalani, 5- Purnima Bannerjee, 6- Leela Roy, 7- G. Durgabai, 8- Hansa Mehta, 9- Kamala Choudhry, 10- Renuka Ray, 11- Malati Choudhury, 12- Dakshayani Velayudhan, 13- Begum Aizaz Rasul, 14- Annie Mascarene and 15- Ammu Swaminathan.
  • The Interim government of India was formed on 2 September, 1946; however, it did not include any member from the Muslim League.
  • Finally on 26 October 1946, 5 Members of the Muslim League were also included in the Cabinet. Interim Cabinet- 1946

Chapter 5

Sources of the Constitution

21 facts · 7 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (8 points)
  • A major portion of the Indian Constitution is borrowed from the Government of India Act 1935 (Blue Print of Indian Constitution).
  • Rule of law, Parliamentary form of government, Cabinet System, Single Citizenship, Bicameral Legislature, Law making procedures, Parliamentary Privileges and prerogative writs are provisions borrowed from the Constitution of Britain.
  • Preamble, Judicial review, Independence of Judiciary, Fundamental rights, the post of Vice-President, the procedure of impeachment of President and removal of Supreme Court and High Courtjudges are provisions taken from the Constitution of the USA.
  • DPSP (Directive Principle of State Policy), method of election of President and nomination of members to the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) are provisions inspired by the Constitution of Ireland.
  • Federation with a strong centre, Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, residuary powers to be vested in the centre and appointment of Governors by the centre are provisions borrowed from Constitution of Canada.
  • Joint sitting of both houses of the Parliament, language of Preamble, Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse and idea of concurrent list are borrowed from Constitution of Australia.
  • Provision related to Emergency (except Financial emergency) imported from Constitution of Germany. Procedure Established by law from Japan, procedure of the Constitutional Amendment and election of members of Rajya Sabha are borrowed from South Africa.
  • Fundamental Duties and the ideals of Justice (social, economic and political) in the preamble are imported from the USSR. The Republican system, principle of liberty, equality and fraternity in the preamble are borrowed from the Constitution of France.

The Constitution is supreme in India's political system: the supreme law that frames all government institutions, rights, directives and duties. Must know

Articles of the Constitution

25 facts · 4 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (111 points)
  • There were 22 parts, 395 Articles and 8 schedules in the original copy of the Constitution.
  • A number of Articles were added and removed later through amendments.
  • At present, there are around 468 articles, but these are added in the form of Articles inserted with alphanumeric suffixes such as 21A, 43B, etc. of the original Articles (395).

Chapter 8

Schedules

54 facts · 12 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (23 points)
  • The Constitution of India at the time of its adoption had only 8 schedules but, there are 12 schedules in our Constitution at present.
  • First Schedule – States and Union Territories with territorial demarcation.
  • Second Schedule – Provisions relating to the salary, emoluments and allowances of the various office bearers of the Union of India.
  • Third Schedule – Forms of oaths and affirmations of the various office bearers of the Union of India.
  • Fourth Schedule – Allocation of seats in the Council of States to the States and Union Territories.
  • Fifth Schedule – Provisions relating to the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes.
  • Sixth schedule – Provisions relating to the administration of tribal areas in the States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
  • Seventh Schedule – Division of powers between the Union and the States. It contains three lists-

(i) Union List – Originally 97 subjects (presently 98) and only the centre has the power to make laws on these subjects.

(ii) State list – Originally 66 subjects (presently 59) and Primarily the States have the power to make laws on these subjects.

(iii) Concurrent list – Originally 47 subjects(presently 52) and on these subjects the centre and the States both have the power to make laws.

  • Radio and Television, stock exchanges and future market, share market, Post Office, Banking, Census, Insurance, Defence, Railways and corporation taxes, etc. come under the Union list.
  • Police, Public health and sanitation, gas, agriculture, railway police, prisons, Panchayati Raj or local Government and land reforms etc., come under the State list.
  • Economic and Social planning, Criminal procedure, population control and family planning, education, Forests, Marriage, Divorce and adoptions etc., come in the Concurrent List.
  • Eighth Schedule – Languages recognised by the Constitution. Originally, it had 14 languages, but presently, there are 22 languages.
  • Sindhi was added by the 21st Constitutional Amendment Act of 1967.
  • Konkani, Nepali and Manipuri were added by the 71st Amendment Act, 1992 and Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali were added by the 92nd Amendment Act, 2003. Oriya was renamed as Odia by the 96th Amendment Act, 2011.
  • Ninth Schedule – Validation of certain Acts and Regulations (originally 13 but presently 284).
  • It was added by the 1st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951.
  • Tenth Schedule – Provision relating to disqualification of the members of Parliament and State Legislatures on the ground of defection.
  • It was added by the 52nd Amendment Act 1985. Also known as the Anti–Defection Law.
  • Eleventh Schedule – Specifies the power, authority and responsibilities of Panchayats. It has 29 subjects. It was added by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
  • Twelfth Schedule – Specifies the power, authority and responsibilities of Municipalities, etc. It has 18 subjects. It was added by the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.

12 Schedules now; originally 8; 9th added by 1st Amendment 1951 (validation of Acts); 10th by 52nd Amendment 1985 (anti-defection).

Chapter 9

The Preamble

35 facts · 10 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (16 points)
  • The Objectives Resolution was moved to the Constituent Assembly on 13th December 1946 by Pt. Jawahar Lal Nehru, and it was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 January 1947. Later, this Resolution became the foundation of the Preamble.
  • The words ‘Socialist’, ‘Secular’, and ‘Integrity’ were incorporated in the Preamble by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act 1976.
  • The Preamble declares India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic. It secures for all its citizens, justice of three types – social, economic and political. It is very helpful in the legal interpretation of the Indian Constitution.
  • In the words of Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, “The Preamble to our Constitution expresses what we had thought or dreamt so long”.
  • The Supreme Court accepted it as a part of the Constitution in the Keshavanand Bharti case(1973).
  • Before this, in the Berubari case (1960), the Preamble was not considered a part of the Constitution.
  • In Golaknath vs State of Punjab (1967), the preamble was considered as the core soul of the Constitution.
  • In Bommai vs Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court again gave the concept that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution.
  • It is non – justiciable in nature.
  • It talks about the freedom of faith, belief, worship, expression and thought.
  • It also ensures dignity and equal status and opportunities for all.
  • It is called the soul of the Constitution.
  • Dr. B. R. Ambedkar called the right to Constitutional remedies (Art. 32) as the heart and soul of the Constitution.
  • K. M. Munshi called the Preamble the political horoscope.
  • Subhash Kashyap said that, ifthe Constitution is the body then the preamble is the soul; ifthe Constitution is the building then the preamble is the foundation stone.
  • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar said that “the Constitution is a pious paper.”

Preamble gives the adoption date → 'this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949'.

Chapter 10

The Governance System

79 facts · 7 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (22 points)
  • A Government is an institution or a system made of a group of people that takes care of or manages a country or a State. Every Government has its own Constitution or a set of fundamental principles that it follows to ensure effective governance.
  • An autocracy is a form of Government where the supreme power or rule is in the hands of one individual or entity.
  • Autocracy includes an absolute monarchy, where a family or a group of families rule a country.
  • The post of monarch is inherited in an absolute monarchy.
  • Monarchy is one of the oldest forms of Government. Now, autocracy also includes dictatorship.
  • Dictatorship is a form of Government in which an individual possesses absolute power without any effective limitations.
  • Democracy is the most widely adopted system of Governance at present. In this form of Government, the final power resides with the people.
  • The State has four essential elements - Population, Territory, Government and Sovereignty. Sovereignty is the most important element.
  • India, before 1947, was not a State because though it had three other elements,
  • i.e. population, territory and Government; the fourth and most important one, i.e. sovereignty, was missing because of British control over India.
  • There are mainly two types of systems of Governance – Parliamentary and Presidential.
  • India follows a Parliamentary form of government which is influenced by the Parliamentary system of the United Kingdom.
  • In the Parliamentary system, members of the executive branch are usually taken from the Legislature and are also accountable to the legislature. The Parliamentary system of Government is also known as the Cabinet form of Government.
  • The government is responsible to the popular House of the legislature and remains in power till it has the support of a majority of members in that House. Thus, the Cabinet form of Government is a mechanism to ensure the collective responsibility of the Government to House of the people.
  • In India, the Cabinet is headed by the Head of the Government, the Prime Minister.
  • The Head of the State is the President.
  • India is a Democratic Republic where the Supreme power is vested in the people of India.
  • The Indian political system does not provide for a unified authority but makes a division of powers between the Union and the States.
  • The Indian Constitution has both Federal and Unitary features. In its Federal characteristic, it has a written Constitution, division of powers between centre and States, independent judiciary and bicameral legislature, etc.
  • However, it also includes unitary features like single citizenship, the appointment of Governors by the President, Declaration of emergency and the power of parliament for implementation of international agreements.
  • In the Presidential form of Government, the President is the head of the executive branch.
  • The best example of the Presidential form of Government is the Government of the USA. Granville Austin described Indian Federalism as Cooperative Federalism. K.C. Wheare describes it as Quasi – federal. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar stated that the Constitution has not been set in a tight mould of federalism, that is, it contains both federal and unitary features.

Chapter 11

National Symbols

14 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (25 points)
  • The National Flag (Tricolour) is rectangular in shape and consists of three colours.
  • The ratio of the length of the flag to its width is 3:2.
  • The colour of the top band is Indian saffron (Kesariya) (symbol of strength and courage), the middle band is white (symbol of peace and truth) and the bottom is Indian green (symbol offertility, growth and auspiciousness of the land).
  • In the centre of the white band is a navy blue wheel, which represents the Ashoka chakra. It has 24 spokes, and its design is that of the wheel, which appears on the abacus of the Sarnath lion capital of Ashoka.
  • It is the symbol of Justice- (Wheel of the law/Dharma Chakra).
  • The National flag was designed by Pingali Venkayya.
  • The present design of the national flag was adopted by the constituent assembly on 22 July, 1947.
  • The description of the importance of three colours and a wheel (chakra) in our national flag by Dr. S. Radhakrishnan is mentioned and reproduced in the Flag code of India.
  • The state emblem is an adaptation of the Sarnath lion capital of Ashoka.
  • It was adopted by the Government of India on 26 January, 1950.
  • The words 'Satyameva Jayate' from Mundaka Upanishad are inscribed at the bottom in the Devanagari Script.
  • The National Anthem of India 'Jana Gana Mana.....' was officially adopted by the constituent assembly on 24th January, 1950.
  • It was first sung on 27th December, 1911 at the Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress (President- Pt. Bishan Narayan Dar).
  • It was authored by Rabindra Nath Tagore. The Playing time of the full version is approximately 52 seconds.
  • The song 'Vande Mataram' was adopted as the national song by the constituent assembly on 24 January, 1950. It is taken from the novel "Anand Math" authored by Bankimchandra Chatterjee.
  • It was first sung at the 1896 session of the Indian National Congress (President -Rahimatullah Sayani).
  • The National Calendar based on the Saka era (Chaitra as its first month and Falgun as the last) was adopted on 22nd March, 1957 along with the Gregorian Calendar. Generally, the month of Chaitra begins on 22 March, but in the leap years, it begins on 21 March.
  • The National Flower of India is the Lotus (Nelumbo nucifera Gaertn). The National fruit is Mango (Magnifera Indica).
  • The National tree is the Banyan tree (Ficus benghalensis).
  • While the government has clearly stated in the Rajya Sabha that no notification has been issued regarding India having a National flower.
  • The National Animal is the magnificent Tiger (Panthera tigris).
  • The National Bird is the Indian Peacock (Pavo cristatus).
  • The National Aquatic animal is the mammal Ganges River Dolphin (Platanista gangetica).
  • The river Ganga was declared the national river by the government of India in the year 2008.
  • The Government of India declared the Independence Day (15 August), Republic Day (26 January) and the Birth Anniversary of Mahatama Gandhi (2 October) as National Days.

Chapter 12

States and the Union Territories

50 facts · 12 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (17 points)
  • The Indian Independence Act of 1947 led to the formation of two independent and separate Dominions – India and Pakistan. The Princely States were provided three options – to join India, to join Pakistan or to remain Independent.
  • There were more than 560 princely States within the Indian territory, out of which most joined India, whereas three (Hyderabad, Junagadh and Kashmir) refused to join India.
  • Later on, Hyderabad through military Action, Junagadh through a referendum and Kashmir through the Instrument of Accession (a legal document) executed by Maharaja Hari Singh (ruler of the Jammu & Kashmir) were included in the Indian Union. The Indian Constitution that came into force in 1950 went a step further, recognising four different categories of States and territories in the first Schedule. Part A was comprised offormer British India provinces, which had a governor and a Legislature. Part B was comprised offormer Princely States governed by a 'raj pramukh' while Part C was a combination of Princely States and chief commissioner's provinces governed by a chief commissioner. Part D was comprised of the lone territory of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands administered by the President through a Chief Commissioner/Other authority appointed by him. It was Part C states and part D territories that would go on to form the basis for the creation of Union Territories.
  • As per the Article 1(1) of the Constitution, “India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States” rather than the Federation of States.
  • Article 2 provides for the admission or establishment of New States.
  • Article 3 provides for the power of the Parliament in the formation of New States and alteration of areas, boundaries and names of existing States.
  • Parliament can form new States through a simple majority.
  • Amendments made under Articles 2 and 3 are out of the scope of Article 368.
  • Presently, India comprises 28 States and 8 Union Territories. S.K. Dhar Commission 1948 recommended the reorganization of States on the basis of administrative convenience instead of a linguistic basis.
  • In December 1948, the JVP committee was constituted by the Congress to scrutinize the recommendations of the S.K. Dhar Commission.
  • This committee included Jawahar Lal Nehru, Vallabh Bhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramaiya.
  • The committee, in its report presented in April 1949, officially rejected the demand for the reorganization of the States on linguistic basis.
  • Although the demise of Potti Sriramulu after the 56-day-long hunger strike forced the Indian Government for the formation of Andhra Pradesh on linguistic basis in October, 1953.
  • Andhra Pradesh is the first State of India formed on the linguistic basis.
  • A States Reorganisation Commission under the Chairmanship of Fazal Ali was constituted for the formation of new States in 1953.
  • Two other members of this Commission were – K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru.
  • Some of the recommendations of this commission were implemented in the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

Chapter 13

The Citizenship

13 facts · 3 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (16 points)
  • The Constitution deals with the citizenship from Articles 5 to 11 under Part II.
  • India, like Britain, adopted the system of single citizenship.
  • Article 11 empowers the Parliament to make laws regarding citizenship.
  • The Indian Citizenship Act was passed by Parliament in 1955.
  • It prescribes five ways ofacquiring citizenship – (1) By Birth,

(2) By Descent, (3) By Registration, (4) By Naturalisation and (5) By incorporation of territory.

  • The Indian Citizenship Act 1955, prescribes three ways of losing citizenship, whether acquired under the Act or prior to it under the Constitution – (1) By Renunciation, (2) By Termination and (3) By Deprivation.
  • Article 6 provides for the rights of citizenship of certain persons who have migrated to India from Pakistan.
  • Article 7 provides for the rights of citizenship of certain migrants to Pakistan.
  • Article 8 provides for the rights of citizenship of certain persons of Indian origin residing outside India.
  • Persons voluntarily acquiring citizenship of a foreign State are not to be citizens as mentioned in Article 9.
  • As per the Section 5 (1) (a) of the Citizenship Act 1955, a person of Indian origin can acquire citizenship by registration if a person of Indian origin who has been a resident of India for 7 years before applying for registration. The Act has been amended: in 1957, 1985, 1986, 1992, 2003, 2005 and 2015, 2019.
  • Under section 7A of The Citizenship Act, 1955 (inserted by 'The Citizenship Amendment Act, 2015) the Central government may, subject to such conditions, restrictions and manner as may be prescribed, on an application made on this behalf, register as an Overseas Citizen of India cardholder. Under this Amendment Act, it has been provided that no person, who or either of whose parents or grandparents or great grandparents is or has been a citizen of Pakistan, Bangladesh or such other country as the central government may, by notification in the official Gazette, specify, shall be eligible for registration as an overseas citizen of India cardholder under this sub-section.
  • The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 was passed by the Parliament of India on 11 December, 2019. It amended the Citizenship Act, 1955 by providing (section 6B) that illegal migrants of Hindu, Sikh, Jain, Parsi, Buddhist and Christian religious minorities who had come to India on or before 31 December, 2014 due to religious persecution from Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan shall not be treated as illegal migrants for the purpose of this Act, and by enabling grant of citizenship via certificates of registration/naturalisation, but subject to conditions. (Muslims are not included in this Act). This Act came into force on 10 January, 2020. Citizenship (Amendment) Rules, 2024 have been notified on 11 March 2024, which are rules for implementing section 6B of the Citizenship Act, 1955.
  • This Act does not apply to the tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Tripura, which are included in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution.
  • This Act does not apply even in the areas coming to the inner line under the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873.

Citizenship → Part II of the Constitution, Articles 5 to 11. Must know

Chapter 14

Fundamental Rights

137 facts · 28 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (41 points)
  • The first explicit Demand for the Fundamental Rights (FR) came in the form of the "Constitution of India Bill, 1895" which was inspired by Bal Gangadhar Tilak. The Motilal Nehru Report of1928 demanded inalienable Fundamental Rights for the people of India.
  • The Congress adopted a resolution on Fundamental Rights at the Karachi Session of 1931, presided over by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.
  • The Fundamental rights are enshrined in Part III of the Constitution from Articles 12 to 35.
  • Originally, the Constitution provided for seven fundamental rights – (1) Right to Equality, (2) Right to Freedom, (3) Right against Exploitation, (4) Right to Freedom of religion, (5) Cultural and Educational rights, (6) Right to Property and
  • (7) Right to Constitutional remedies.
  • However, the Right to Property was deleted from the list offundamental rights by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.
  • Now, the right to property is a legal right under Article 300-A in Part XII of the Constitution. Fundamental Rights are the guarantee against the arbitrary actions of the State.
  • The enforcement of fundamental rights (except the rights under Articles 20 and 21) can be suspended during the operation of a national emergency, by an order of the president. These rights are justiciable.
  • Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution are often compared with the Bill of Rights in the Constitution of the U.S.A. Part III of the Indian Constitution is rightly regarded as the Magna Carta of India.
  • The Fundamental Rights are defended and guaranteed by the Constitution.
  • Article 14 provides for Equality before the law and equal protection of the laws.
  • The Right to equality is enshrined in the Constitution from Articles 14 to 18.
  • Prohibition of discrimination only on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (Article 15).
  • Article 16- Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment.
  • Article 17- Abolition of untouchability and prohibition of its practice.
  • Article 18 – Abolition of titles except military and academic.
  • The Right to freedom is described in Articles 19 to 22. Article 19 guarantees all citizens six rights.
  • These are – Article 19(1) (a) – Right to freedom of speech and expression, Article 19 (1) (b) – Right to assemble peacefully and without arms, Article 19(1) (c) – Right to form associations or unions or cooperative societies, Article 19(1) (d) – Right to move freely throughout the territory of India, Article 19 (1)(e) – Right to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India and Article 19(1) (g) – Right to practice any profession or to carry on any occupation, trade and business.
  • Article 20 provides for protection in respect of conviction for offences.
  • Protection of life and personal liberty is described in Article 21.
  • Eighty
  • – Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 made free and compulsory education (for all children of the age 6 to 14 years) a fundamental right and added Article 21A.
  • Article 22 provides for protection against arrest and detention in certain cases. Right against exploitation is described in Articles 23 and 24.
  • Article 23 provides for the prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour.
  • Article 24 provides for the prohibition of employment of children (below the age of 14 years) in factories, etc.
  • The Right to freedom of religion is described in Articles 25 to 28.
  • Articles 29 and 30 are related to the cultural and educational rights of minorities.
  • Article 32 provides for Constitutional remedies.
  • Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 as 'the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it/ "heart and soul".
  • The Supreme Court (under Article 32) can issue writs only for the enforcement of fundamental rights, and the High Courts (under Article 226) can issue writs not only for the enforcement of fundamental rights but also for any other purpose.
  • Five kinds of writs are mentioned in Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution:
  • (1) Habeas Corpus (to have the body of) – The writ of Habeas Corpus can be issued against both public authorities as well as private individuals who have detained another person to produce the body of the latter before it.
  • Ifthe detention is found to be illegal, the detained person would be set free.
  • This writ is the bulwark of individual liberty against arbitrary detention.

(2) Mandamus (We command) – It is a command issued by the court against a public official, any public body, a corporation, an inferior court, a tribunal or a government, asking them to perform official duties that one has failed or refused to perform.

(3) Prohibition (to forbid) – It is issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal to prevent the latter from exceeding its jurisdiction or usurping a jurisdiction that it does not possess.

(4) Certiorari (to be certified) – It is issued on the grounds of excess of jurisdiction or lack of jurisdiction or error of law. It is issued by a higher court to a lower court to transfer a case pending with the latter to itselfor to quash the order of the latter in a case.

(5) Quo – Warranto (By what authority or warrant) – It is issued by the court to enquire into the legality of the claim of a person to a public office.

  • Article 358 provides for the suspension of provisions of Article 19, during emergencies.
  • Article 359 provides for the suspension of the enforcement of fundamental rights except Articles 20 and 21 during emergencies (after the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act).
  • The Supreme Court, in its judgment in the case of Bachan Singh Vs State of Punjab, held that the sentencing discretion inherent in section 302 of the IPC is not violative of Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Indian Constitution.

Best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy → separation of powers (restrains power); not a committed judiciary or centralisation.

Chapter 15

Directive Principles of State Policy

53 facts · 14 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (26 points)
  • The Directive Principles of State Policy are mentioned in Part IV of the Indian Constitution from Articles 36 to 51.
  • The idea of Directive Principles of State Policy is borrowed from the Irish Constitution.
  • Article 37 deals with the application of the principles contained in this part.
  • The Directive Principles are non – justiciable.
  • The Constitution (Article 37) itself says that these principles are fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
  • They embody the concept of a ‘Welfare State’.
  • Article 38 says, the State is to secure a social order for the promotion of the welfare of the people.
  • Article 39A, added by the 42nd Amendment, provides for the equal justice and free legal aid to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities.
  • Organisation of Village Panchayats (Article 40).
  • Right to work, to education and to public assistance in certain cases (Article 41).
  • According to the Article 42, the State shall make provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief. According to Article 43, the State shall endeavour to secure, for all workers, work and living wage, and to promote the cottage industry.
  • Participation of workers in the management of industries (Article 43 A).
  • Promotion of cooperative societies (Article 43 B).
  • Uniform Civil Code for the citizens (Article 44).
  • The State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education to children below the age of six years (Article 45).
  • Promotion of educational and economic interests of scheduled castes, scheduled tribes and other weaker sections (Article 46).
  • It is the duty of the State to raise the level of the nutrition and the Standard of living and to improve public health (Article 47).
  • Organisation of Agriculture and Animal Husbandry (Article 48).
  • Article 48A provides for the protection and improvement of the environment and safeguarding of forests and wild life.
  • Article 49 provides for the protection of monuments, and places and objects of national importance.
  • Separation of judiciary from executive (Article 50).
  • Promotion of international peace and security (Article 51). Difference between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles

Chapter 16

Fundamental Duties

25 facts · 8 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (15 points)
  • The Fundamental Duties in the Indian Constitution are inspired by the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR.
  • These were added on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee through the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.
  • This amendment added a new part (Part IV A) which consists of only one article, that is, Article 51 A.
  • Presently, the number of Fundamental Duties, as per the Article 51 A, is 11, whereas originally, at the time of its inclusion in the Constitution, the number was 10. The 11th Fundamental Duty was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002.
  • According to Article 51 A, it shall be the duty of every citizen of India –

(a) To abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem;

(b) To cherish and follow the noble ideas which inspired our national struggle for freedom;

(c) To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India;

(d) To defend the Country and render national service when called upon to do so;

(e) To promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India; to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women;

(f) To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture;

(g) To protect and improve the natural environment- including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and to have compassion for living creatures;

(h) To develop the scientific temper, humanism and spirit of inquiry and reform;

(i) To safeguard public property and to abjure violence; (j) To Strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective Activity.

(k) Who is a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years (added by 86 Amendment Act, 2002).

Fundamental Duties (Article 51-A, Part IV-A; 42nd Amendment 1976, Swaran Singh Committee) are non-justiciable: no legal process to enforce them; not correlative to legal duties.

Chapter 17

The President

95 facts · 20 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (38 points)
  • The President of India is the head of the Indian State, the first citizen, and acts as the symbol of unity, integrity and solidarity of the nation.
  • According to Article 52, ‘There shall be a President of India’.
  • According to Article 53, the executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President and shall be exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with this Constitution.
  • According to Article 54, the President shall be elected by the members of an electoral college consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of the Legislative Assembly of the States.
  • 70th Amendment Act, 1992 (effective from 01- 06-1995) provided for the inclusion of the elected members of legislative assemblies of the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union territory of Puducherry in the electoral college for the election of the President.
  • Nominated members and members of Legislative Councils do not participate in the election of the President.
  • According to Article 55(3), the election is held in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and the voting is done by secret ballot.
  • All doubts and disputes in connection with the election of the President are enquired into and decided by the Supreme Court, whose decision is final.
  • The Election of the President cannot be challenged on the grounds that the electoral college was incomplete. (due to any vacancy of members)
  • Article 58 describes the eligibility criteria (a citizen of India, has completed the age of 35 years and is qualified for election as a member of the House of the People, and is not ineligible due to holding any office of profit under Article 58(2)) for election as President.
  • Further, the nomination of a candidate for election to the office of President must be subscribed by at least 50 electors as proposers and 50 electors as seconders.
  • Every candidate has to make a security deposit of Rs. 15000. The security deposit is liable to be forfeited in case the candidates are not elected and the number of valid votes polled by such candidates does not exceed one-sixth of the number of votes necessary to secure the return of a candidate at such election.
  • The President's term of office is five years from the date on which he enters his office (Article 56).
  • According to Article 56 (1)(a), the President submits his resignation in writing under his hand addressed to the Vice- President of India. The Vice-President shall immediately inform, about the resignation, to the speaker of the Lok Sabha (Under Article 56(2)).
  • Further under Article 56(1)
  • (b) he can also be removed from the office by the process of Impeachment (mentioned under Article 61)
  • The Article 57 defines the eligibility of re-election, to the post of the President, for a person. The only ground for impeachment specified in the Art. 61(1) is the violation of the Constitution.
  • No President has so far been impeached.
  • When a vacancy occurs in the office of the President due to his resignation, removal, death or otherwise, the Vice–President acts as the President until a new President is elected.
  • Further, when the sitting President is unable to discharge his functions due to absence, illness or any other cause, the Vice–President discharges his functions until the President resumes his office.
  • In case the office of the Vice–President is vacant, the Chief Justice of India (or if his office is also vacant, the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court available) acts as the President or discharges the functions of the President.
  • According to Article 59(1), if any person who is a member of either House of Parliament or a House of the State legislature is elected as President, he is deemed to have vacated his seat in that house on the date on which he enters upon his office as President.
  • The oath of office to the President is administered by the Chief Justice of India (Art. 60).
  • Currently, the salary of the President is 5 Lakh per month. It is paid from the Consolidated Fund of India.
  • According to Article 77, the conduct of businesses of the Government of India is formally done in the President's name.
  • He can summon a joint sitting of both the houses of Parliament (Art.108).
  • When a bill is sent to the President after it has been passed by the Parliament, he can give his assent to the bill or withhold his assent to the bill, or return the bill (if it is not a money bill) for reconsideration by the Parliament. However, if the bill is passed again by the Parliament, with or without amendments, the President has to give his assent to the bill.
  • A bill becomes an Act after the assent of the President.
  • The President cannot return a money bill for reconsideration.
  • Money bill is introduced in the Parliament, that too in Lok Sabha only with his prior recommendation.
  • He can promulgate ordinances when the Parliament is not in Session (Art.123).
  • These ordinances must be approved by the Parliament within six weeks from its reassembly.
  • He can also withdraw an ordinance at any time.
  • Article 72 of the Constitution empowers the President to grant pardons to persons and to suspend, remit, respite, reprieve or commute sentences in certain cases.
  • He has the power to consult the Supreme Court (Art. 143).
  • He can declare any area as a scheduled area and has powers with respect to the administration of scheduled areas and tribal areas. He is the supreme commander of defence forces (Army, Navy and Air-force) of India.
  • The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 made a provision that made the President bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.
  • The 44thAmendmentAct, 1978 (enacted by the Janta Party Government) authorized the President to require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice either generally or otherwise. However, he shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration.

Head of the Indian Republic (Head of State) → President of India; first President Dr. Rajendra Prasad (26 Jan 1950 to 13 May 1962). Must know

Chapter 18

The Vice-President

18 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (18 points)
  • The post of the Vice–President of India is modelled on the lines of the American Vice–President.
  • Vice–President is next to the President in the official order of precedence.
  • According to Article 63, there shall be a Vice–President of India.
  • According to Article 64, the Vice–President is the ex–officio Chairman of the Council of States.
  • While acting as the President or discharging the functions of the President, the Vice– President does not perform the duties of the office of the chairman of Rajya Sabha (Article 64, proviso) and he is not entitled to the salary or allowance payable to the Chairman of Rajya Sabha but the salary and allowances of the President.
  • He is elected by members of an electoral college consisting of the Members (both elected and nominated) of both houses of Parliament.
  • According to Article 66 (1), the election of Vice-President is held in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and the voting is done by secret ballot.
  • The eligibility for election as Vice-President (a citizen of India, should have completed 35 years of age, and should be qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha) is mentioned in Article 66 (3).
  • The Vice-President draws his salary (4 lakh per month) in his capacity as the ex–officio chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
  • The constitution has not fixed any emoluments for the Vice–President in that capacity.
  • According to Article 67, the Vice–President holds office for a term of five years. According to Article 67(a), a vice president may, by writing under his hand addressed to the president, resign his office.
  • According to Article 67 (b) he can be removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by an absolute majority and agreed to by the Lok Sabha, but no resolution for this purpose shall be moved unless at least fourteen days' notice has been given of the intention to move the resolution.
  • The Vice – President of India and their terms of office is as follows

Chapter 19

The Council of Ministers

81 facts · 7 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (18 points)
  • The Central Council of Ministers includes Prime Minister, Cabinet ministers, Ministers of State and Minister of State (independent).
  • According to Article 74(1), there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President, who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice. However, the President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice, and the President shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration (added through the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act 1978).
  • The advice tendered by Ministers to the President shall not be inquired into in any court [Article 74 (2)].
  • According to Article 75
  • (1), the Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President and other Ministers shall be appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.
  • According to Article 75 (1A), the total number of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, in the Council of Ministers shall not exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha. This provision was added by the 91st Amendment Act, 2003.
  • As per Article 75(2), the Ministers shall hold office during the pleasure of the President.
  • The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
  • The term ‘Cabinet’ was mentioned only in clause
  • (3) of the Article 352 of the Constitution and it was inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act. It did not find a place in the original content of the Constitution.
  • Cabinet includes Cabinet Ministers and the Prime Minister.
  • Due to the Ministerial Responsibility, for every act of the bureaucrats, the concerned Minister is answerable to the Parliament.
  • The Central Cabinet Secretariat is directly under the control of Prime Minister. Its administrative head is the Cabinet Secretary, who is the ex-officio chairman of the Civil Services Board.
  • A person who is not a member of either house of the Parliament can also be appointed as a minister, but within six months, he must become a member (either by election or by nomination) of either house of the Parliament, otherwise he ceases to be a minister.
  • The President administers the oath of office and secrecy to the Prime Minister and other ministers.
  • The Prime Minister is the Chairman of Union Cabinet meetings.
  • According to Article 78, it shall be the duty of the Prime Minister to communicate to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers and to furnish such information relating to the administration of the affairs of the Union and proposals for legislation as the President may call for. The Prime Minister submits his resignation to the President. The ministries of departments are created by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister under the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules 1961, which are rules made by the President under Article 77 of the Constitution. There are 53 ministries at present in the Government of India.
  • The number of Ministries at the centre on 15 August 1947 was 18.

Article 300 → the legal name of the Government of India is 'The Union of India'.

Chapter 20

The Attorney-General and the C.A.G.

37 facts · 14 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (22 points)
  • The Indian Constitution provides for the office of the Attorney General for India.
  • He is the highest law officer in the country.
  • The President shall appoint a person who is qualified to be appointed a judge of the Supreme Court to be the Attorney General for India [Article 76 (1)].
  • It shall be the duty of the Attorney-General to give advice to the Government of India upon such legal matters, and to perform such other duties of a legal character, as may from time to time be referred or assigned to him by the President [Article 76(2)].
  • In the performance of his duties, the Attorney-General shall have the right of audience in all courts in the territory of India [Article 76(3)].
  • The Attorney-General shall hold office during the pleasure of the President, and shall receive such remuneration as the President may determine [Article 76 (4)].
  • He has the right to speak and to take part in the proceedings of both the houses of the Parliament or their joint sitting but without the right to vote.
  • He enjoys all the privileges and immunities that are available to a member of Parliament.
  • According to Article 165 (1), the Governor of each State shall appoint a person who is qualified to be appointed a judge of a High Court to be Advocate-General for the State. He advises the State Governments on legal matters.
  • He is the first legal adviser to the State Government.
  • He shall hold office during the pleasure of the Governor.
  • According to Article 148(1), there shall be a Comptroller and Auditor-General of India who shall be appointed by the President and shall only be removed from office in like manner or on the like grounds as a judge of the Supreme Court.
  • The Comptroller and Auditor-General shall not be eligible for further office either under the Government of India or under the Government of any State after he has ceased to hold his office [Article 148(4)].
  • He holds office for a period of 6 years or up to the age of 65 years.
  • He can be removed by the President on the basis of a resolution passed to that effect by both the Houses of Parliament with special majority, either on the grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
  • He is the guardian of the public purse and audits the entire financial system of the country at both the levels – the Centre and the State.
  • He is called as the ‘friend, philosopher and guide’ of the Public Accounts Committee.
  • He submits his audit reports relating to the accounts of the centre to the President who shall, in turn, causes them to be laid before both the houses of the Parliament [Article 151(1)].
  • He submits his audit reports relating to the accounts of a State to the Governor who shall, in turn, place them before the State Legislature [ Article 151(2)].
  • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar said that the CAG is probably the most important officer under the Constitution of India.
  • The Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act came into effect in 1971. This Act was amended in 1976 for the separation of accounts from audit.
  • The CAG submits three audit reports to the President, an audit report on appropriation accounts, an audit report on finance accounts, and an audit report on public undertakings. The President causes these reports to be laid before both the Houses of the Parliament. After this, the Public Accounts Committee examines them and reports its findings to the Parliament.

Chapter 22

The Parliament (1)

84 facts · 23 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (36 points)
  • Parliament is the legislative organ of the Union Government.
  • Articles 79 to 122 in Part V of the Indian Constitution deal with the Parliament.
  • According to Article 79, the Parliament of India consists of the President and the two houses - House of the People and the Council of States.
  • Lok Sabha is also known as the "House of the People".
  • Its maximum strength is 550. At present, it has 543 (States-524, UTs-19) members.
  • Out of 550 members, at most 530 members are representative of states, 20 members are representative of Union territories. If, in the opinion of the President, there is not enough representation of the Anglo-Indian Community in the Lok Sabha, then he could nominate two members of that community to the Lok Sabha. In this regard, the arrangements related to the Anglo-Indian Community have not been extended beyond the stipulated date (25 January, 2020) by 'The Constitution (One Hundred and Fourth Amendment) Act, 2019' [The Constitution (One Hundred and Twenty-Sixth Amendment) Bill, 2019]. Thus, the arrangements for the nomination of two members of the Anglo-Indian community in the Lok Sabha have ended.
  • The allocation of state-wise seats in the Lok Sabha is based on the Census of 1971.
  • According to the 84th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001, the next assessment shall be held after the year 2026.
  • In Lok Sabha seats are allotted on the basis of the population.
  • The normal tenure of Lok Sabha is 5 years from the date of its first meeting after the general elections but it can be dissolved by the President in between.
  • Under the Article 83(2) Proviso, Lok Sabha can be extended during the time of National Emergency for one year at a time.
  • In any case of extension, it can't continue beyond the period of 6 months after the emergency has ceased to operate.
  • The qualifications of a person in order to be elected a member of Lok Sabha are (a) He must be a citizen of India and (b) He must not be less than 25 years. (c) He must make and subscribe to an oath (d) He must possess other qualifications prescribed by the Parliament by law.
  • According to Article 93, the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker are elected by Lok Sabha from among its members.
  • Suspension of Lok Sabha (Adjournment/Adjournment Sine die of Lok Sabha sitting) is called up by the Speaker, whereas prorogation and dissolution of Loksabha is called up by the President of India.
  • According to Article 94 (b), the Speaker of Lok Sabha addresses his resignation in writing to the Deputy Speaker and vice-versa.
  • The speaker of Lok Sabha is removed from his Post by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of Lok Sabha and such resolution shall not be moved until and unless a 14-day advance notice is given.
  • While a resolution of removal of the Speaker or Deputy Speaker is under consideration, the Speaker/Deputy Speaker concerned can not preside but both have the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of the house.
  • While the proposal of removal of the Speaker or Deputy Speaker is in process, the Speaker or Deputy Speaker (as the case may be) have the right to vote in first instance but not in the case of equality of votes.
  • The Speaker of Lok Sabha uses his casting vote only in case of a tie.
  • Lok Sabha Secretariat directly functions under the Speaker of Lok Sabha.
  • After the general elections, the Protem Speaker administers the oath to the newly elected members of Lok Sabha.
  • As provided by the Constitution, the Speaker of the last Lok Sabha vacates his office immediately before the first meeting of the newly elected Lok Sabha. Therefore, the President appoints a senior member of the Lok Sabha as the Pro-tem Speaker.
  • Article 85(1) empowers the President to summon each house of the Parliament if he thinks fit.
  • In any case, the interval between the two consecutive sessions of the houses cannot be more than six months. (
  • Thus as per the Constitution, it is mandatory for Lok Sabha to meet at least twice a year.
  • According to Article 100(3), the quorum of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha shall be 1/10th of the total members of the respective houses.
  • Uttar Pradesh has the highest number of Lok Sabha seats
  • (80) followed by Maharashtra (48) and West Bengal (42). In January, 2022 the Election Commission of India (ECI) has increased the expenditure limits for candidates, contesting in the Lok Sabha and Legislative Assembly polls. The ECI hiked the poll expenditure limit upto Rs. 95 lakh from the existing Rs. 70 Lakhs for the Lok Sabha election. For the state assembly elections, the expenditure limit has been enhanced to Rs. 40 lakh from Rs. 28 lakh. For small states, revised expenditure for the Loksabha is increased by Rs. 75 Lakhs from Rs. 54 Lakhs. While, in the case of small state assembly it is increased to Rs. 28 Lakhs from the previous limit of Rs. 20 Lakhs.
  • First Lok Sabha elections were held from 25 October, 1951 to 21 February, 1952.
  • The elections were conducted for 489 seats.
  • First Meeting of Lok Sabha took place on 13th May, 1952.
  • Ganesh Vasudev Mavlankar became the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha and remained in this post till his death on 27 February, 1956. M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar was the speaker for the remaining tenure of the first Lok Sabha. In 1954, the first resolution/motion for removal of the speaker was brought against the first Speaker of Lok Sabha, G.V. Mavlankar, by Vigneshwar Missir (Socialist Party M.P. from Bihar), J.B. Kriplani and some other members of Opposition in the Lok Sabha which was rejected by the Lok Sabha.
  • First Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha was M.A. Ayyangar.
  • The First woman speaker of Lok Sabha was Meira Kumar.
  • The Speaker of the present (18th) Lok Sabha is Om Birla.

Chapter 23

The Parliament (2)

48 facts · 8 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (26 points)
  • The Upper House of the Parliament is also known as the Rajya Sabha. It is also known as the 'Council of States'.
  • The Maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is fixed at 250. According to Article 80, the Rajya Sabha consists of not more than 238 members from the States and Union Territories (elected indirectly) and 12 other members are nominated by the President from amongst the persons having special knowledge or practical experience in the field of literature, science, art and social service (Present Strength is 245, out of which 12 are nominated members).
  • Representatives of each state shall be elected by the elected members of the legislative assembly of the state in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote.
  • Only 3 Union territories (Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir) out of 8 have representatives in Rajya Sabha.
  • Rajya Sabha is a Permanent house. Hence it is not subject to dissolution.
  • As nearly as possible 1/3rd members of the Rajya Sabha retire at the end of every second year.
  • The term of its members is 6 years.
  • A Person to be elected as a member of Rajya Sabha must fulfil two criteria- (1) he must be a citizen of India and
  • (2) he must not be less than 30 years of age. In addition to the prior two conditions, he must be an elector for a parliamentary constituency in India.
  • The Vice-President of India is the ex officio chairman of the Council of States/Upper House of Parliament.
  • When the Vice-President acts as the President he shall not be entitled to get the salary and allowances of the Chairman of Rajya Sabha. For this period, he receives salary and allowances of the President.
  • Rajya Sabha elects a deputy chairman from amongst its members.
  • The Deputy Chairman gives his resignation in writing to the Chairman.
  • Rajya Sabha has the power to remove the Deputy Chairman from his post, by a resolution passed by the absolute majority of the total members of Rajya Sabha. Such resolution can be moved only after giving at least 14 days' notice.
  • When the post of Chairman is vacant, the deputy chairman will perform the duties of the chairman.
  • While presiding over the Rajya Sabha, the Deputy Chairman can't vote in general, he can only exercise a casting vote in case of a tie.
  • When a resolution to remove the Vice President from his office is under consideration, he will not be presiding as the Chairman and when a resolution of removal of the Deputy Chairman is under consideration, he will not be presiding as the Deputy Chairman.
  • The representation of states in Rajya Sabha is given in proportion to their population.
  • For a quorum, there must be the presence of one-tenth of the total number of members in the Rajya Sabha.
  • The Representation of People Act 1951 (through an amendment in 2003) made a provision that any person can contest from anywhere for Rajya Sabha even ifhe is a resident of any other state. Now for contesting Rajya Sabha elections, a person must be an elector in a parliamentary constituency anywhere in India.
  • The 4th Schedule of the Indian Constitution enumerates the allocation of Rajya Sabha seats for states and union territories.
  • Article 249 states that ifthe Rajya Sabha passes a resolution with a 2/3 majority of its members present and voting, the Parliament can make laws in the national interest regarding the subjects of the state list, which are specified in the resolution.
  • It is valid for a period of1 year, but it can be extended by passing a resolution.
  • Article 250 empowers the Parliament to legislate with respect to any matter in the state list if the proclamation of emergency is in operation but, six months after the emergency ceases to operate, it automatically expires.
  • Article 252 empowers the Parliament to legislate for two or more states by consent and adoption of such legislation by any other state.
  • According to Article 253, Parliament has the power to make any law for the whole or part of the territory of India for implementing international agreements or conventions with any other country or any decision made at any international conference.

Rajya Sabha maximum strength → 250 (238 States/UTs + 12 nominated, Art 80); present 245 (225 States, 8 UTs, 12 nominated).

Chapter 24

The Parliament (3) Conduct of Business and Legislative Procedure

108 facts · 22 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (25 points)
  • The Parliament of India is the supreme legislative body.
  • India has a parliamentary system of Government based on the Westminster model.
  • The Right to amend the constitution is vested in the Parliament under Article 368.
  • Maximum time gap between the two sessions of parliament is 6 months.
  • Lok Sabha speaker, Deputy speaker, Secretary General, Rajya Sabha chairman, Deputy chairman etc. are called officials of parliament.
  • There are usually three sessions in a year, i.e. Budget session, Monsoon session and Winter session.
  • If any member of Parliament remains absent for 60 days from all meetings without informing to the respective house, then the House may declare his seat vacant.
  • Article 105 of the Indian Constitution lays down the privileges and immunities of the members of Parliament.
  • For making International treaties effective, the Parliament can make laws in the state list without the consent of the state.
  • Speaker or chairman of the House can prohibit any member and allow any other member to speak. This is called Yielding the floor.
  • When a member of parliament changes party allegiance, leaving one political party and joining another political party in the Parliament, it is called Crossing the floor.
  • Zero Hour is a unique feature of the Parliamentary system of India. It can be a maximum of one hour, which is around 12 noon to 1:00 pm in Lok Sabha (its duration is not fixed in the Rules).
  • A money bill can only be introduced in Lok Sabha and that too on the recommendation of the President of India. It cannot be introduced in Rajya Sabha.
  • Rajya Sabha cannot reject or amend a money bill and must return it within 14 days, after which, Lok Sabha may accept or reject its recommendations. If the money bill is not returned within 14 days, it is deemed passed by both Houses in the form passed by Lok Sabha.
  • According to Article 108, the President summons both the Houses for ajoint sitting to resolve the deadlock between the two houses over the passage of a bill.
  • According to Article 118(4) the speaker shall preside over a joint sitting of two houses of parliament.
  • The Joint sitting of two Houses of Parliament is called up only for ordinary bills or non-money financial bills. The Joint sitting of two houses of Parliament is not called for Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills.
  • Since 26 January, 1950 joint sitting of two Houses has been invoked only for three bills- the first one was in 1961 for the Dowry prohibition bill, second one was for the Banking service commission (repeal) Bill in 1978 and third one in 2002 for the prevention of terrorism Bill.
  • Any ordinary bill can be introduced in any house of parliament.
  • The Speaker has power to decide whether a bill is a money bill or not.
  • To withdraw the funds from the Consolidated Fund of India, the government needs to pass appropriation bills.
  • According to Article 116 of the Indian Constitution, when an appropriation bill is not passed and the government needs funds then Lok Sabha has the power to withdraw funds from the consolidated fund of India through a Vote on Account, for a fixed period of time.
  • The Estimates Committee is the largest among the Financial committes of Parliament. It consists of 30 members (all from the Lok Sabha). There is no Rajya Sabha member in the Estimates Committee.
  • The Secretariat of the Indian Parliament is free from the Government.
  • Indian Parliament established control over administration through parliamentary committees.

Lok Sabha (Art 81): up to 530 State members + up to 20 UT members (the 'X') + 2 Anglo-Indians earlier (ended 25 January 2020); Rajya Sabha: 250 (238 + 12).

Chapter 25

Parliamentary Committees

31 facts · 6 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (15 points)
  • The Parliament is assisted by a number of Committees in the discharge of its duties. These committees are appointed or elected by Houses of the Parliament or nominated by the Speaker / Chairman. They perform their work under the direction of the Speaker / Chairman and submit their report to the House, or to the Speaker / Chairman as applicable.
  • Mainly the parliamentary committees are of two kinds – Standing committees and Ad-hoc committees.
  • The Standing committees are permanent (constituted every year or periodically) and work on a continuous basis while the Ad-hoc committees are temporary and cease to exist on completion of the task assigned to them.
  • Standing Committees are-
(i)Financial Committees
(ii)Department-related Standing Committees. (Total 24)
(iii)Committee of Enquiry
(iv)Committees to Scrutinise and Control
(v)Committees relating to the day-to-day business of the

House.

(vi) Housekeeping Committees or Service Committees.

  • Financial committee includes the Public Accounts Committee, Estimates Committee and Public Undertakings Committee.
  • Most of the standing committees, leaving some committees, consist of members from Lok Sabha and Rajya sabha in the ratio of 2:1.
  • The Public Accounts committee consist of 22 members (15 from Lok sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha). It examines various expenditure reports and accounts under the purview of the Parliament.
  • The Estimates Committee consists of 30 members elected every year by the Lok Sabha from among its members. All of its members are from Lok sabha.
  • Its function is to suggest alternative policies in order to bring about efficiency and economy in administration and to report improvements in organizations, efficiency or administrative reform, consistent with the policy underlying the estimates, may be effected.
  • Public Undertakings Committee consists of 22 members (15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha). It analyses the accounts and workings of the state-owned PSU firms. It also checks the disinvestment policies of the various PSUs. Committee to Inquire includes the committee on petitions, the committee on privileges and the ethics committee.
  • The Petition committee in Lok Sabha consists of15 members, while the petition committee in Rajya Sabha consists of 10 members.
  • Public Accounts Committee submits its report to the Lok Sabha Speaker. (Ordinarily Presents reports to the House; only when the House is not in session, it may present the report to the Speaker and later present it to the House). Generally, a member from the opposition in Lok Sabha is appointed as the chairperson of this committee by the speaker of Lok Sabha. There are a total of 24 Departmentally Standing Committees (DRSCs). Out of 24, 8 under Rajya Sabha and 16 under Lok Sabha.

Parliament controls the administration through Parliamentary Committees (Public Accounts, Estimates, Standing Committees).
