Chapter 26

Parliamentary Act

88 facts · 4 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (14 points)
  • The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 was introduced in 1954 and came into force on 1 June, 1955 (Repealed w.e.f. 5 August, 2011).
  • All the punishable offences under the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 are cognizable and triable summarily.
  • The trials of crime under the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 are done by a First Class Judicial Magistrate and in the case of Metropolis, it is done by Metropolitan Magistrate.
  • The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 was brought into force on 26 October, 2006.
  • The Criminal Tribes Act was first enacted in 1871.
  • The Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 has been applicable in India since 30 January 1990. To implement the objectives of The Scheduled Castes and The Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, the central government has the power to make rules by notification in the Official Gazette.
  • Section 18 of The Scheduled Castes and The Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 prohibits anticipatory bail to the accused.
  • According to Rule 7(1) of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Rules, 1995, an offence committed under this Act shall be investigated by a police officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police.
  • Under section 14 of this Act, the State Government, for the purpose of providing speedy trial, is empowered to constitute a court of session, with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the High Court, to be a special court for each district to try the offence under the SC & ST Act.
  • Hindu Marriage Act, Hindu Succession Act and The Commission of SATI (Prevention) Act were enforced in 1955, 1956 and 1988, respectively.
  • Right to Information came fully into force on 12 October 2005. The Right to Information is a legal right. According to the Supreme Court, it is also a fundamental right. The use of the Right to Information Act is to obtain Information from the public authority.
  • Namit sharma V/s Union of India case is related to the Right to Information Act 2005. The Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan is an Indian social movement and grassroots organization best known for its demand for the Right to Information Act. The Right to Information (Amendment) Act, 2019 removed the previous provision i.e., the Chief Information Commissioner (CIC) and Information Commissioner (IC) at the Central and State levels will hold office for a term of five years and substituted it by term as may be prescribed by the Central Government.
  • The National Green Tribunal was established on 18 October, 2010, under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.
  • The provision of the Panchayats (extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 or PESA is a law enacted by the Parliament of India ensuring self-governance through traditional gram sabhas for people living in the Scheduled Areas of India.

Chapter 27

The Supreme Court

104 facts · 19 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (35 points)
  • An Integrated Judicial system has been established under the Indian Constitution in which the Supreme Court is at the top.
  • Below the Supreme Court there are various High Courts.
  • This single system of the Judiciary has been adopted from the Government of India Act 1935.
  • The Supreme Court of India was inaugurated on 28th January 1950.
  • Articles 124 to 147 in Part V of the Indian Constitution deal with the Supreme Court.
  • The Supreme Court of India consists of the Chief Justice of the India and up to 33 other judges.
  • Earlier there were 30 Judges and a Chief Justice. Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019 increased the number of Judges including Chief Justice from 31 to 34. The President of India appoints the judges of the Supreme Court.
  • The President appoints a Chief Justice after consultation with the other judges of the Supreme Court of India and the judges of the high courts.
  • The person to be appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Court must be a citizen of India and he should be, for at least 5 years, a Judge of a High Court or two or more such courts in succession; or he has been for at least ten years an advocate of a High Court or of two or more such courts in succession; or he must be a distinguishedjurist in the opinion of President.
  • No minimum age is prescribed for the appointment of judges of the Supreme Court.
  • Parliament has the power to increase the number of Judges in Supreme Court.
  • A person appointed as the Judge of the Supreme Court has to make and subscribe an oath or affirmation before the President.
  • Judges can give their resignation in writing to the President.
  • Judges of the Supreme Court can be removed by the President after the recommendation of the Parliament (address by each House).
  • Recommendation (Address) of Parliament for the removal of Judges must be passed by a special majority in each House of the Parliament.
  • The recommendation of Parliament is presented to the President in the same session.
  • The grounds on which removal of judges takes place are proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
  • These removals can be declared unconstitutional and illegal in the state of being extraordinary.
  • The Judges of the Supreme Court retire at the age of 65 years.
  • Salary and other allowances of the Supreme Court Judges are determined by Parliament.
  • Under Article 127, the Chief Justice of India can designate a judge of a High Court as an Ad hoc Judge of the Supreme Court for a temporary period to complete the quorum of the Judges in the Supreme Court (with the previous consent of the President and after consultation with the Chief Justice of High Court concerned).
  • The bench hearing a case related to the interpretation of the Constitution should have at least 5 judges.
  • According to Article 129, the Supreme Court is a Court of Record.
  • It has the power to punish for its contempt.
  • Court of Record means a court whose proceedings are kept as a record and are available as an evidence offact. Article 131 deals with the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. Disputes between the Government of India and any of the States of the Union, the government of India and any State or States on one side and any other State or States on the other side or between two or more States comes under the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (only if the dispute involues a question on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends).
  • Articles 132 to 136 deal with the Appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
  • The Supreme Court under its extraordinary powers conferred by Article 136 can interfere to quash the decision of a quasi - Judicial tribunal when the tribunal has either exceeded its jurisdiction or has approached the question referred to in a manner likely to result in injustice.
  • Article 137 provides that the Supreme Court has the power to review any judgement pronounced or order made by itself.
  • The concept of Judicial review is based on the Procedure established by law and supremacy of the Constitution.
  • The last authority to interpret the Constitution is the Supreme Court. It is called as the Guardian of the Indian Constitution.
  • According to Aarticle 143, the President may seek the opinion of the Supreme Court on any question of law or fact of public importance on which he thinks it is expedient to obtain such an opinion or on any dispute arising out of the pre-constitutional treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement or other similar instruments. In first case the Supreme Court may tender or refuse to answer but in second case Supreme Court is bound to tender its opinion.
  • The Supreme Court can send any case to any court of the country.
  • The source of the Doctrine of Basic Structure of the Indian Constitution is Judicial interpretation.
  • Article 141 of Indian Constitution stipulates that the decision of the Supreme Court would be binding upon all courts within the territory of India.
  • In the Keshvananda Bharati Case (1973), the Supreme Court propounded the Doctrine of the Basic Structure of the Indian Constitution.

Supreme Court of India → inaugurated 28 January 1950.

Key facts from the book (22 points)
  • The Constitution of India envisages the same pattern of government in the states as that for the centre, that is, a parliamentary system. Articles 153 to 167 in Part VI of the Constitution deal with the Government of the state.
  • The Governor is the executive head of the state. Generally, a person is the governor of only one state and after the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1956, the same person can be appointed as the governor of two or more States.
  • The Governor is appointed by the President of India (Article 155).
  • He holds office for a term of 5 years from the date on which he enters upon his office.
  • However, his tenure is subject to the pleasure of the President [Article 156(1)].
  • Further he can resign at any time by addressing a resignation letter to the President [Article 156(2)].
  • According to Article 157, the qualifications for the post of the Governor are - (i) He should be a citizen of India, and (ii) age over 35 years. Jammu & Kashmir Reorganisation Act 2019 reorganised the state of Jammu & Kashmir into: (i) the Union territory of Jammu & Kashmir with a legislature, and (ii) the Union Territory of Ladakh without a legislature. Both the newly created Union Territories will be administered by the President through a Lieutenant Governor appointed by him.
  • All the executive works of the state is formally done in the name of the Governor.
  • The Chief Minister of the National Capital Territory of Delhi is appointed by the President (Article 239 AA).
  • The salary, allowances and other expenditures related to the Governor are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of each state [Article 202(3)(a)].
  • The Governor has the power to appoint the Chief Minister and the Council of Ministers on the advice of the Chief Minister [Article 164(1)].
  • He is an integral part of State Legislative Assembly and has the right to address and send messages and of summoning/proroguing and dissolving the State Legislative Assembly.
  • The Governor has the right to nominate one-sixth of the members of the legislative council. Governor of a state, if he is of the opinion that the Anglo-Indian community needs representation in the Legislative Assembly of the state and is not adequately represented therein, could nominate one member of that community to the Assembly. It is noteworthy that the arrangements of nominating representatives of the Anglo-Indian community in the state Legislative Assemblies have not been extended beyond the stipulated date (25 January, 2020) by 'The Constitution (One Hundred and Fourth Amendment) Act, 2019. Thus, the arrangements of nomination of one member of the Anglo-Indian Community in the Legislative Assemblies has ended.
  • A person who has the qualification required for the judge of a High Court can be appointed as the Advocate General by the Governor (Art. 165).
  • When a bill is sent to the Governor after it is passed by State Legislature, he can give his assent to the bill, or return the bill (if it is not money bill) for reconsideration, or reserve the Bill for the consideration of the President.
  • However if the bill is passed again by the state legislature the governor may give his assent to the bill or reserve the Bill for the consideration of the President.
  • According to Article 201, if a bill is reserved by the Governor for the consideration of the President, then the President will declare whether to give assent to the bill or not.
  • Article 202 (3) (a) the emoluments and allowances of the Governor and other expenditure relating to office are charged on the consolidated fund of the state.
  • The Governor can promulgate an ordinance when the state legislature is not in session (Article 213), and only if the circumstances require immediate action.
  • He can grant pardons, reprieves, respites and remission of punishment or suspend, remit and commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the state extends (Article 161).
  • Sarojini Naidu was the first woman to be appointed as the Governor of any state.
  • She was the governor of Uttar Pradesh (United Provinces) from 15th August, 1947 to 2 March, 1949.

Chapter 29

The State Legislature

69 facts · 9 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (29 points)

Legislative Council

  • As per Article 169, the Parliament has power of the abolition and the creation of the Legislative Council in a state, if the Legislative Assembly of the State passes a resolution to that effect, by a majority of the total membership of the Assembly and by a majority of not less-than two-thirds of the members of the Assembly, present and voting.
  • Article 171 of the Indian Constitution makes provision for the Composition of Legislative Councils in the states.
  • Only 6 States have Legislative Councils at present, these are Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh. It is a permanent House.
  • The tenure of its members is 6 years.
  • According to Article 171 (1) the maximum strength of the Legislative Council shall not be more than one-third of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly, but not less than 40.
  • Uttar Pradesh with 100 members in the Legislative Council is the largest Legislative Council.
  • According to Article 171

(4) the elected members of Legislative Council are elected in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and by secret ballot.

  • A person to be elected a member of the Legislative Council must not be less than 30 years of age.
  • Ifthe question arises as to whether a member of the house of the legislature of a state has become subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in clause (1) of the Article 191, the question shall be referred for the decision of the governor and his decision shall be final. Before giving any decision on any such question, the Governor shall obtain the opinion of the Election Commission and shall act according to such opinion. Article 171 (3) Provides for the election of the nearest 5/6 members of the legislative council and the remaining members to be nominated by the Governor. However, the composition of the Legislative councils in the states is under the provisions of Section 10 and Schedule 3 of 'The Representation of the People Act, 1950' (as amended from time to time) made by the Parliament under Article 171 (2).
  • The State Legislative Council has the power to remove its Chairman or Deputy Chairman from their post by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council.
  • Article 191 of the Constitution of India deals with the disqualification of the members of the State Legislature. Legislative Assembly
  • Articles 168 to 212 in Part VI of the Indian Constitution deal with the State Legislature.
  • According to Article 168 the State legislature, in specified States, consists of Legislative Council, Legislative Assembly and governor of the state, and in the other States it consists of Legislative Assembly and the Governor of the State.
  • The Legislative Assembly of each state shall be composed of Members elected by direct election on the basis of Universal Adult Suffrage from territorial constituencies.
  • The maximum number of members of the Assembly shall not be more than 500 nor less than 60 members, generally.
  • The smallest assembly among Union territories is Puducherry (33) and in states it is Sikkim (32).
  • Uttar Pradesh has the largest Legislative Assembly with 403 members.
  • The Election Commission of India conducts the elections for the state legislatures.
  • According to Article 170 (2) Each state shall be divided into territorial constituencies in such a manner that the ratio between the Population of each constituency and the number of seats allotted to it shall, so far as practicable, be the same throughout the state.
  • The Speaker of the assembly exercises a casting vote in case of equality of votes.
  • The speaker establishes the contact between the house and the Governor.
  • In the absence of a speaker, the deputy speaker works as the speaker of the Assembly.
  • According to the 84th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001, the number of members in State Assemblies will remain the same until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 2026 have been published.
  • Under section 14(3) of the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 the number of assembly members in Jammu & Kashmir UT is 90 elected and 5 nominated [plus 24 vacant election constituencies fall in areas occupied by Pakistan (POK)].
  • Only three Union Territories (Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu & Kashmir) have legislative assemblies. Article 173 lays down the qualifications of a person to be a member of the legislative assembly (a) He must be a citizen of India, and (b) He must not be less than 25 years of age.
  • According to Article 332 the Constitution provides for the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the legislative assembly in proportion to their population.
  • The Rights and Functions of the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly are the same as those of the Speaker of the lower House of the Parliament.

Chapter 30

The High Court

41 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (32 points)
  • According to the Constitution of India, the High Court occupies the top position in the judicial administration of the State.
  • The Constitution of India provides for a High Court for each state, but the 7th Constitution Amendment Act of 1956, authorised the Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more States, or for two or more States and a Union territory.
  • Articles 214 to 231 in part VI of the Constitution deal with the organisation, independence, jurisdiction, powers, procedures and so on, of the High Courts.
  • Article 214 states that every state will have a High Court.
  • Article 215 states that every High Court will be Court of Record.
  • Article 216 states that every High Court will consist of a chief justice and such other judges as the President may from time to time deem necessary to appoint.
  • A High Court is a Court of Record which means that thejudgements proceedings and acts of the High Court are recorded for perpetual memory and testimony.
  • These records are admitted to be ofevidentiary value and cannot be questioned when produced before any subordinate court. They are recognised as legal precedents and legal references and the court also has powers to punish for contempt of itself.
  • The judges of the High Courts are appointed by the President.
  • The President appoints them after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the governor of the State, and (for Judges other than the Chief Justice) the Chief Justice of High Court concerned.
  • A judge holds the office until he attains the age of 62 years.
  • He can resign from his office by writing to the President.
  • A judge can be removed from his office by the President on the recommendation of the Parliament.
  • The President can issue a removal order only after an address by the Parliament has been presented to him in the same session for such removal passed with a special majority (a majority of the total membership of each House and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting in each House).
  • Just like a Supreme Court Judge, a High Court Judge can be removed from his office on the grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
  • A person to be appointed as a judge of a High Court - should be a citizen of India, he should have held a judicial office in the territory of India for at least ten years or he should have been an advocate of a high court (or high courts in succession) for at least ten years.
  • According to Article 223, the President can appoint a judge of a High Court as an acting chiefjustice of the High Court to perform the duties of the office of Chief Justice, when the office of the Chief Justice is vacant or the Chief Justice of the High Court is temporarily absent or the Chief Justice is unable to perform his duties of his office.
  • Article 226 of the Constitution empowers the High Court to issue writs for the enforcement of the Fundamental Rights of the persons or for any other purpose. Article 227 states that Every High Court shall have superintendence over all courts and tribunals (except relating to the Armed Forces) throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction.
  • At present there are 25 High Courts and 7 of them have jurisdiction over more than one state/Union Territories.
  • Delhi, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh are the Union Territories with their own High Court. Delhi has its own; Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh share a common High Court.
  • The other Union territories fall under the jurisdiction of different state High Courts.
  • The Parliament can extend the jurisdiction of a High Court.
  • The institution of the High Court originated in India in 1862. The High Courts were set up at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras.
  • In 1866, the High Court of Judicature for the North Western Provinces came into existence at Agra. Later, the seat of the High Court for the North-Western Provinces was shifted from Agra to Allahabad in 1869.
  • Article 233 (1) states that the appointment, posting and promotion of district judges in a state are made by the Governor of the state in consultation with the High Court.
  • Article 235 empowers the High Court to have control over all other subordinate courts in that state.
  • In India a person can be detained under Preventive Detention generally for a maximum period of 3 months, under certain conditions, it may exceed 3 months.
  • Lok Adalats (People’s Court) is one of the alternative dispute resolution mechanisms in India, it is a forum where cases pending or at a pre-litigation stage are settled.
  • A Lok Adalat can take up civil cases (including marriage & family) and compoundable criminal cases.
  • A Lok Adalat is usually presided over by a sitting or retired judicial officer as the chairman with two other members, a lawyer and a social worker (composition is not fixed).
  • The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 provides for establishment of Gram Nyayalayas at the grass-root level for the purpose of providing access to justice to the citizens at their doorstep.
  • The Gram Nyayalaya has jurisdiction over both civil and criminal cases (only such disputes and cases as are specified in the Act's Schedule).

Number of Judges in a High Court → decided by the President; each HC has a Chief Justice and such other Judges as the President appoints (Article 216).

Don't confuse Not Parliament or the CM: the President fixes High Court strength.

Chapter 31

The Centre-State Relation

53 facts · 7 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (36 points)
  • The Constitution of India being Federal in structure, divides all powers (legislative, executive and financial) between the Centre and the States.

Legislative Relations

  • Articles 245 to 255 in Part XI of the Constitution deal with legislative relations between the centre and the States.
  • According to Article 245 (1), the Parliament can make laws for the whole or any part of the Territory of India and the State Legislature can make laws for the whole or any part of the state.
  • Article 247 empowers the Parliament to provide for the establishment of certain additional courts.
  • Article 248 deals with Residuary powers of legislation, the exclusive power to make laws with respect to any matter not enumerated in the concurrent or State list is vested in the Parliament.
  • Article 246 deals with subject matters of laws made by Parliament and by the legislatures of the States.
  • The Constitution provides for a three-fold distribution of legislative subjects between the centre and the state i.e. List I (the Union list), List II (the State list), List III (the Concurrent List). The 7th schedule of the Constitution deals with the division of powers between the centre and the state.
  • 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016, inserted new Article 246A: Notwithstanding anything contained in Article 246 and 254, Parliament, and subject to clause (2), the legislature of every state, have the power to make laws with respect to goods and services tax imposed by the Union or by such State.
  • Article 249 deals with the Power of Parliament to legislate with respect to goods and services tax provided under Article 246A or any matter in the state list in the national interest.
  • If the Rajya Sabha declares by resolution that it is necessary in the national interest that Parliament should make laws on a matter in the state list, then the Parliament becomes competent to make laws on that matter.
  • Such a resolution must be supported by not less than 2/3rd of the members present and voting.
  • Article 250 (1) empowers the Parliament to legislate with respect to goods and services tax provided under Article 246A or any matter in the state list if a proclamation of emergency is in operation, Article 251 states that if there is an inconsistency between laws made by Parliament under Art. 249 & Art 250 and laws made by the legislature of States, then the laws made by the Parliament shall prevail.
  • Article 252 deals with the power of Parliament to legislate for two or more States by consent and adoption of such legislation by any other state.
  • Article 253 deals with legislations giving effect to international agreements. The Parliament can make laws on any matter in the state list for implementing the international treaties, agreements and conventions. This provision enables the Central Government to fulfil its international obligations and commitments.

Administrative Relations:

  • Articles 256 to 263 in Part XI of the Constitution deal with the administrative relations between the Centre and States.
  • Article 256 deals with the obligations of States and the Union.
  • The executive power of a State shall be so exercised as to ensure compliance with the laws made by Parliament and any existing laws which apply in that State.
  • Article 257 deals with the control of the Union over States in certain cases.
  • Article 258 deals with the power of the Union to confer powers, etc, on States in certain cases.
  • Accordingly the President may, with the consent of the State government, entrust to that government functions in relation to any matter to which the executive power of the Union extends.
  • Article 262 (1) deals with Adjudication of disputes relating to water of inter-state rivers or valleys.
  • Article 263 allows the President to establish an Inter-state Council to investigate and discuss subjects of common interest between the Centre and the States. Such a council was set up on 28 May, 1990.

Financial Relations:

  • Articles 264 to 293 in Part XII of the Constitution deal with centre-state financial relations.
  • Article 265 of the Indian Constitution deals with the levy of tax. The article States that “No tax shall be levied or collected except by the authority of law.”
  • Article 266 (1) of the Constitution of India deals with the establishment of a Consolidated Fund of India, where all revenues received by Union Government as well as all loans and all money received by the Union Government in repayment of loans shall form the part of the fund. The Contingency Fund of India is established under Article 267
  • (1) of the Constitution. By The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Article 279A was added for the Goods and Services Tax Council.
  • According to Article 267 (2) the legislature of the State may by law establish a Contingency Fund in the nature of an imprest to be entitled the Contingency Fund of the State.
  • Article 275 deals with the Grants allocated by the Union to certain States.
  • A new Article 269A has been inserted into the Constitution by 'The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016. This Article deals with levy and collection of goods and services tax in the course of inter-state trade or commerce.
  • According to Article 280 (1) of the Constitution of India, a Finance Commission is to be constituted by the President within 2 years of commencement of the Constitution of India and thereon every 5th year or at such earlier time as he considers necessary. The Finance Commission of India is considered a quasi-judicial body because it possesses certain powers of a civil court.
  • According to Article 281, the President shall cause every recommendation of the Finance Commission to be laid before both the Houses of the Parliament along with an explanatory memorandum as to the actions taken on its recommendations.
  • In 1983 the Central Government appointed a three-member Commission on Centre-State Relations under the Chairmanship of R.S. Sarkaria a retired Judge of the Supreme Court. Hence the name Sarkaria Commission was given. B. Shivraman and S.R. Sen were the other two members of this Commission. The final Report was submitted in January, 1988 (report contained 247 recommendations spreading over 19 chapters).
  • The Rajamannar Committee and the Punchhi Commission are also associated with Centre-State relations.

Centre-State relations (Part XI) → shaped by Constitutional provisions, the planning process, conflict of political interests and desire to dominate (all four).

Chapter 32

Emergency Provisions

29 facts · 6 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (37 points)
  • The Emergency provisions are contained in Part XVIII of the Constitution from Articles 352 to 360. These provisions enable the Central Government to meet any abnormal situations effectively.
  • The Constitution stipulates three types of emergencies –

(i) An emergency due to war, external aggression or armed rebellion (Art. -352).

(ii) An Emergency due to failure of Constitutional machinery in the state (Art. - 356).

(iii) Financial Emergency due to a threat to the financial stability or credit of India (Art. - 360).

  • During an Emergency, the Central government becomes all powerful and the executive power of the Union extends to the giving of directions to any State as to the manner in which the executive power of the State is to be exercised.
  • Under Article 352, the President can declare a national emergency when the security of India or a part of it is threatened by war or external aggression or armed rebellion.
  • The Proclamation of Emergency must be approved by both the Houses of Parliament by the special majority required by Article 352(6) within one month from the date of its issue.
  • If the proclamation of emergency is issued at a time when the Lok Sabha has been dissolved or the dissolution of the Lok Sabha takes place during the period of1 month without approving the proclamation, then the proclamation survives for 30 days from the first sitting of the Lok Sabha after its reconstitution and ceases unless Lok Sabha also approves it within those 30 days, provided that the Rajya Sabha has in the meantime approved it.
  • If approved by both the Houses of Parliament the emergency continues for 6 months from the date of passing of the Second approving resolution and may be extended for further six-month periods by resolutions of both Houses passed with the special majority under Article 352 (6).
  • During a National Emergency, the Parliament becomes empowered to make laws on any subject mentioned in the State list.
  • The laws made by Parliament on State subjects become inoperative six months after the emergency has ceased to operate. The President can issue an ordinance on state subjects also, if the Parliament is not in session.
  • According to Article 354 (1) while the proclamation of National Emergency is in operation, the President can modify the Constitutional distribution of revenues between the Centre and the States. This modification operates only for a period not extending beyond the end of the financial year in which the proclamation ceases, and every such order must be laid before each House of Parliament.
  • According to Article 83 (2), while a proclamation of National Emergency is in place, the life of the Lok Sabha may be extended beyond its normal term (5 years) by a law of Parliament for one year at a time (for any number of times).
  • However this extension cannot continue beyond a period of six months, after the emergency has ceased to operate.
  • Articles 358 and 359 describe the effect of a National Emergency on Fundamental Rights. Article 358 deals with the suspension of enforcement of the Fundamental Rights guaranteed by Article 19 due to war or external aggression. No separate order for their suspension is required.
  • Article 359 deals with the suspension of enforcement of other Fundamental Rights (Except those guaranteed by Articles 20 & 21).
  • Article 359 authorises the President to suspend the right to move any court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights during a National Emergency.
  • The National Emergency has been proclaimed 3 times so far – in 1962, 1971 and 1975.
  • The President Rule under Article 356 is imposed in case of failure of the Constitutional machinery in the State.
  • Notably in the case of the President’s Rule the President can act either on a report of the Governor or otherwise too (i.e even without the Governor's report).
  • Under this arrangement the President may acquire all or any of the powers of the state government concerned.
  • The President (actually on behalf of him, the Governor)dismisses the state council of ministers headed by the Chief Minister.
  • During this time the Parliament passes the state legislative bills and the state budget.
  • A Proclamation imposing Presidential Rule must be approved by both the Houses of the Parliament within two months from the date of its issue.
  • If approved by both the Houses of the Parliament the President's rule continues for 6 months.
  • It can be extended for a maximum period of 3 years with the approval of the Parliament, every six months.
  • Every resolution approving the proclamation of President’s Rule or its continuance can be passed by either house of the Parliament only by a simple majority. For any extension beyond 1 year, Article 356(5) imposes conditions that must also be met: a National Emergency is in operation and the Election Commission of India certifies difficulty in holding State Legislative Assembly elections.
  • Article 360 of the Indian Constitution deals with Financial Emergency.
  • Article 360 empowers the President to proclaim a Financial Emergency ifhe is satisfied that a situation has arisen due to which the financial stability or credit of India or any part of its territory is threatened.
  • A proclamation of financial emergency must be approved by both the Houses of Parliament within two months from the date of its issue.
  • Once approved by both the Houses of the Parliament, the financial emergency continues indefinitely till it is revoked.
  • During a financial emergency, the centre acquires full direction-based control over the States in financial matters.
  • No financial emergency has been declared so far.
  • K.M. Nambiar, while criticising the emergency powers of the President, called it is “ a fraud on the Constitution.”
  • The phrase ‘armed rebellion’ was inserted by the 44th Amendment Act of1978, replacing the original phrase ‘internal disturbance.’
  • According to Article 355, it is the Duty of the Union to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbances and to ensure that the Government of every State is carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution.

Three emergencies → National Emergency (Art 352), President's Rule on failure of state constitutional machinery (Art 356), Financial Emergency (Art 360).

Chapter 33

The Finance Commission

15 facts · 6 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (11 points)
  • Article 280 of the Constitution provides for a Finance Commission which is constituted by the President of India every fifth year or at an earlier time that he considers necessary.
  • The Finance Commission is required to make recommendations regarding the distribution of the net proceeds of taxes to be shared between the Centre and States, the allocation between the States of the respective shares and the principle that should govern the grants-in-aid to the States by the Centre, measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement resources of Panchayats and Municipalities and any other matter referred by the President in the interest of sound finance.
  • First Finance Commission was constituted vide presidential order dated 22 November, 1951 under the chairmanship of Shri K.C. Neogy on 6th April, 1952.
  • The chairman of the 14th Finance Commission was Shri Y.V. Reddy.
  • 14th Finance Commission recommended an increase in the share of states in the net proceeds of taxes to 42 percent from the then existing 32 percent.
  • The recommendations of the 14th Finance Commission were enforced for the period of five years (2015-20).
  • The 15th Finance Commission was constituted under the chairmanship of N.K. Singh.
  • The tenure for the enforcement of recommendations of the 15th Finance Commission was from the year 2020-21 to the year 2025-26 but the commission submitted two reports - the first report consisted of recommendations for the financial year 2020-21 and the final report with recommendations for 2021-26.
  • The Sixteenth Finance Commission was constituted on 31st December, 2023 under Arvind Panagariya former Vice-Chairman, NITI Aayog.
  • The State Finance Commission is a constitutional body.
  • The Finance Commission constituted under Article 280(1) consists of a chairman and four other members appointed by the president.

Chapter 34

The Planning Commission / NITI AAYOG

19 facts · 8 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (11 points)
  • The Planning Commission was established by an executive resolution of the Government of India on 15 March, 1950.
  • It was neither a Constitutional body nor a statutory body.
  • It was established on the recommendation of an advisory planning board chaired by K.C. Neogy. Prime Minister used to be its ex-officio chairman.
  • First Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission was Guljari Lal Nanda.
  • Its main function was to assess the resources of the country and prepare five-year plans for the central government for balanced utilisation of those resources.
  • The Planning Commission was replaced by 'NITI Aayog' on 1 January, 2015.
  • NITI refers to the Nation al Institution for Transforming India.
  • The current Vice Chairman of NITI Aayog is Dr. Suman K. Bery.
  • Its Chief Executive Officer is B.V.R. Subrahmanyam.
  • The rank and status of its vice-chairperson is equivalent to a Cabinet Minister.
  • The National Development Council was established on 6 August, 1952.

Chapter 35

Lokpal and Important Commissions

107 facts · 10 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (24 points)
  • The earliest democratic institution created in the world for the redressal of citizens' grievances is the Scandinavian institution of Ombudsman.
  • The institution of the Ombudsman was first created in Sweden in 1809. In order to meet the long-standing demand to establish a mechanism for dealing with complaints on corruption against certain public functionaries, the Indian Democratic system proposed the establishment of Lokpal at the centre and Lokayukta at the State level.
  • In its interim report dated 20th October, 1966, under the Chairmanship of Morarji Desai, the First Administrative Reforms Commission (1966- 1970) recommended the setting up of Lokpal and Lokayuktas. Later in the year 1967, K. Hanumanthaiah became its Chairman.
  • Bills regarding Lokpal were first introduced in the year 1968, in the Parliament (in the 4th Lok Sabha).
  • However, on 20th August, 1969, the first Jan Lokpal Bill was passed in the Fourth Lok Sabha. In the year 1972, Maharashtra became the first State to establish the institution of Lokayukta. The Lokayukta Act of Maharashtra was enacted on 30 November, 1971 and it came into effect on 25th October, 1972.
  • Although Odisha had passed the Act in this regard in 1970, it came into force in 1983.
  • According to the Uttar Pradesh Lokayukta Act 1975, the Lokayukta submits his report to the Governor.
  • The Governor presents this report in both Houses of the State Legislature. Institution of Lokpal has been established for the first time in India by 'The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013'. The Lokpal consists of a chairperson and not more than eight members. Former Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose was appointed India's first Lokpal.
  • In the year 1993, the Vohra Committee was setup to study the problem of the criminalisation of Politicians and bureaucrats in India.
  • Rajamannar Committee recommended the abolition of Indian Administrative Services and Indian Police Services. In the year 1993, the then- President exercised his powers under Article 123 and promulgated the Protection of Human Rights Ordinance.
  • As a result, the Protection of Human Rights Act came into force on 28th September 1993.
  • The National Human Rights Commission is a statutory (non constitutional) body. This organization was established on 12th October 1993. Its Chairman and members are appointed by the President, on the recommendations of a 6-member committee consisting of the Prime Minister as its head, the speaker of the Lok Sabha, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the Leader of the Opposition in both Houses of the Parliament and the Home Minister.
  • The Function of the Commission is mainly recommendatory in nature. The Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2019 amended the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. Some major amendments are -

(i) The Act provides that a person who has been the Chief Justice of India, or a judge of the Supreme Court will be the chairperson of the NHRC.

(ii) The Act provides for three persons (of which at least one will be a woman) having knowledge of or practical experience in matters relating to human rights to be appointed as the members of the NHRC.

(iii) The Act reduces the term of office of the chairman and members of the NHRC and SHRC to three years or till the age of 70 years, whichever is earlier.

  • The chairperson and members of the State Finance Commission are appointed by the Governor.
  • The Central Information Commission was established by an official Gazette Notification under the provisions of the Right to Information Act 2005. According to the Right to Information Act, 2005 the term of the Chief Information Commissioner was up to 5 years or 65 years of age. According to the Right to Information (Amendment) Act, 2019 the tenure of the Chief Information Commissioner and other Information Commissioners will be determined by the Central Government. In addition to the central and state level, Chief Information Commissioner and other information commissioners will receive the same salary, allowance and other facilities as the Central Government determines.
  • In the year 1979, under the Chairmanship of Bindeshwari Prasad Mandal, the Mandal Commission was established.
  • The main task of this Commission was to identify and recommend steps for the advancement of the socially and educationally backward classes of India.
  • Article 315 of the Indian Constitution deals with the establishment of Public Service Commission for the Union and for the States.
  • The Union Public Service Commission consists of a Chairman and other Members appointed by the President of India, whereas the Chairman and Members of the State Public Service Commission are appointed by the Governor of the State.
  • According to Article 323, the UPSC presents annually, to the President, a report on its performance, whereas the SPSCs present annually, to the Governor a report on their performance.
  • According to Article 322, the expenses of the Union or a State Public Service Commission shall be charged on the Consolidated Fund of India or the Consolidated Fund of State (in case of SPSCs).

Chapter 37

Election Commission

50 facts · 10 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (16 points)
  • Articles 324 to 329 in Part XV of the Constitution deal with the provisions related to the electoral system.
  • According to Article 324, there shall be an election commission, which is a permanent and independent body.
  • This commission is responsible for superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of the electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all elections to the Parliament, the Legislature of every State, the President and the Vice-President.
  • The election commission consists of a Chief Election Commissioner and other election commissioners (the number being decided by the President from time to time) [Art. 324(2)]. The Chief Election Commissioner and other election commissioners are appointed by the president.
  • Till 15 October, 1989 there was only a Chief Election Commissioner, but on 16 October, 1989 two additional election commissioners were appointed for the first time.
  • But these posts were in effect upto the 1st of January 1990.
  • On 1st October 1993, again two additional election commissioners were appointed and since then the election commission has three members. At present, there are two Election Commissioners and one Chief Election Commissioner in the Election Commission. They have equal power and their salary and perks are the same as those of the Judges of the Supreme Court.
  • Their tenure is for 6 years or up to the age of 65 years (whichever is earlier).
  • The chief election commissioner can be removed from his office only in a manner and on the grounds prescribed for the removal of Judges of the Supreme Court [Article 324(5)].
  • Other Election Commissioner or the Regional Commissioner can be removed by the President on the recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner.
  • The notifications for the elections to the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha are issued by the President and for the state legislative assemblies by the Governor.
  • Article 326 mentions the provision of Adult Suffrage. The right to vote in India is a Statutory Right.
  • As per the Representation of the People Act 1951, there is right to vote and to be elected in India.
  • The age for the right to vote was decreased from 21 years to 18 years by the 61st Constitutional Amendment Act 1988 which came into effect from 28 March 1989.
  • The elections to the local bodies (Panchayats and Municipalities) is being conducted by the State Election Commissions.
  • The Delimitation Commission is a commission established by the Government of India. Its main task is to redraw the boundaries of various assemblies and lok sabha constituencies based on the recent census. Till now, the Delimitation commission has been set up for five times (1952, 1963, 1973 and 2002) and the latest in March 2020. The March 2020, Delimitation Commission was constituted via notification for delimitation of the UT of Jammu & Kashmir.

Election Commission → Article 324: superintendence, direction and control of electoral rolls and elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, President and Vice-President. Must know

Political Parties

53 facts · 3 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (18 points)
  • The Party system is a part of the political system.
  • Formation and working of the government in the Democratic political system is done with the help of the Party system.
  • Under the Representation of the People Act 1951, there is a provision for the registration of political parties.
  • Election Commission of India registers the Political Parties.
  • By the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act 1985, Political Parties, for the first time, were given the Constitutional status. This Act came into force on 1 March, 1985.
  • Tenth Schedule which is related to the Anti-defection law, was added to the Indian Constitution by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act 1985.
  • Internal party democracy is used for internal elections in the political parties.
  • It occurs periodically to elect the officials of the political parties.
  • The Election Commission is empowered to grant status to different political parties as national and state parties.
  • Presently 6 political parties are recognised as National-level parties in our country.
  • These are Indian National Congress (INC), Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), Bahujan Samaj Party, Communist Party of India - Marxist (CPI-M), Aam Aadmi Party and National People's Party.
  • In India, elections are held on the basis of Universal Adult Franchise.
  • Political parties have the freedom to establish their own standards, subject to mandatory legal/registration conditions.
  • The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 and its first president was W.C. Banerjee.
  • The word 'National' in Indian National Congress reflects its all-India character and intent to speak for people across India, it was also influenced by the reaction against British Rule.
  • Bharatiya Janata Party was founded in 1980 and its first president was Atal Bihari Vajpayee.
  • The Independent Labour Party was founded by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar in 1936.
  • The Communist Party of India was found ed in 1925 and C.P.I. (Marxist) was founded in 1964.

Chapter 39

Constitutional Amendment

65 facts · 13 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (26 points)
  • Any constitution, even ifit is made wisely, needs amendments in time and circumstances.
  • Indian Constitution is a mixture of rigidity and flexibility.
  • It contains the provision of Amendments in Article 368 of Part-XX of the Indian Constitution.
  • The Indian Constitution can be amended in three different ways.
1.Simple majority
2.Special majority
3.Special majority and by the ratification of not less
  • than one-half of the state legislatures. A Constitutional Amendment bill can be introduced in either House of the Parliament.
  • Constitutional Amendment bill needs to be passed by both the Houses of the Parliament separately with a special majority and there is no provision for the joint sitting of the Houses for the Constitutional Amendment bill.
  • Election of President, Representation of States in the Parliament, Supreme and High Court, power of Parliament to amend the constitution etc, are the subjects that require a special majority of the Parliament and ratification by at least half of the state legislatures for the Amendment.
  • Any amendment in the provision of the Constitution by a simple majority in both the Houses is not included in the amendment under Article 368.
  • These include the provisions regarding admission or establishment of new states, alteration of names, areas, boundaries, etc.
  • The 1st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 added two new Articles i.e. Article 31A and 31B and also the 9th Schedule.
  • 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 is known as a mini-constitution.
  • 52nd Amendment Act is related to the Anti-defection law.
  • 61st Amendment Act, 1988 reduced the voting age from 21 years to 18 years.
  • 69th Amendment Act, 1991 gave Delhi the status of the National Capital Territory of Delhi.
  • 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 added Article 21A, i.e. Right to Education, Provision for Free and compulsory education for children from the age of 6 years to 14 years.
  • The 91st Amendment Act, 2003 amended Articles 75 and 164 and Schedule 10.
  • It inserted a new Article 361B.
  • This Amendment restricts the size of the Council of Ministers, including the Prime Minister to aid and advise the President.
  • That cannot be more than 15% of the total number of members of the House of the People at the Union level and the total number of members of the state legislative assembly at the level of the State.
  • 97th Amendment Act 2011 gave constitutional status to the co-operative societies (Part IX B inserted by the 97th Amendment is now operative only for multi-State Co-operative Societies).
  • 100th Constitutional Amendment Act is related to the India-Bangladesh boundary st
  • treaty.
  • 101 Amendment Act is related to the GST (Goods and Services Tax). The National Commission for Backward Classes has been given constitutional status through the 102nd Amendment Act. The 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 deals with providing 10 percent reservation in government Jobs and education to the Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) of citizens. This EWS category includes citizens other than the classes mentioned in clauses (4) and (5) of Article 15 and clause (4) of Article 16.
  • The Doctrine of basic structure of the Constitution refers to the features of the Constitution which are inviolable and cannot be amended or altered by the Parliament.
  • The doctrine of basic structure was given by the Supreme Court in the famous Keshavananda Bharati case of 1973. The 105th Constitutional amendment amends clauses 1 and 2 of Article 342A and also introduces a new clause 3. It also amends Articles 366 (26C) and 338B(9). It is designed to clarify that states can maintain the 'state list' of OBCs. The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 is the Latest amendment in the Indian Constitution. It reserves one third of all seats for women in Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies, and the Legislative Assembly of the National Capital Territory of Delhi, including those reserved for SCs and STs. This reservation for women shall come into effect after the next delimitation exercise following the first census conducted after the Act's commencement, and shall remain in effect for 15 years from such commencement.

Art 368 → Parliament can amend any part by addition, variation or repeal, except basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973); Parliament is supreme elected body → R explains A.

Chapter 40

Official Language

19 facts · 4 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (16 points)
  • The Official language is mentioned in Part-XVII (Art. 343- 351) of the Indian Constitution.
  • According to Art. 343, the official language of the union shall be Hindi in Devanagari script and the digits used for official purposes shall be an international form of Indian numerals.
  • Under Article 344, the president has the power to form a commission related to the official language. According to Article 344, the President shall at the expiration of five years from the Commencement of the Constitution and there after at the expiration often years from such commencement, by order constitute a commission on official language.
  • The First official language commission under the chairmanship of B.G. Kher was constituted in 1955.
  • According to Art. 344 (4), there is a provision to form a 30- member joint parliamentary committee on official language. The committee consists of20 members from Lok Sabha and 10 members from Rajya Sabha.
  • Any language can be added in the Indian Constitution under the 8th Schedule.
  • Initially only 14 languages were added to the Indian Constitution.
  • 'Sindhi' language was added to the Indian Constitution by the 21st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1967.
  • Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali were added by 71st Constitutional Amendment Act 1992 in 8th Schedule.
  • In 2003, Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali were added by the 92nd Constitutional Amendment. At present, a total 22 languages are there in 8th Schedule. According to Article 345, the legislature of a State may by law adopt any one or more of the languages in use in the State or Hindi as the language or languages to be used for all or any of the official purposes of that State; till such adoption English language shall continue to be used for official purposes.
  • There is a description of official language for communication between two states or between a state and the union in Article 346.
  • According to Article 347, there is a special provision relating to language spoken by a section of population of a state.
  • Hindi was accepted by the Constituent Assembly as the official language on 14th September 1949.
  • 14 September is celebrated as the Hindi Diwas. According to Article 348 (1)
  • (a), all proceedings in the Supreme Court and every High Court shall be done in English language. Under Article 348(2), with the previous consent of the President, the Governor of a State may authorise the use of Hindi or any other language used for any official purposes of the State, in proceedings in the High Court, having its principal seat in that States.
  • According to Article 350 A, there is a provision offacilities for instruction in the mother tongue at primary stage. Article 350B provides for the establishment of a special officer for linguistic minorities. The officer shall be appointed by president and shall investigate all matters relating to safeguards for linguistic minorities, reporting directly to the President.

Art 343(1) → Hindi in Devanagari is the Union's official language; Art 343(2) → English allowed for all official purposes for 15 years from commencement.

Chapter 41

Panchayati Raj and Community Development

165 facts · 29 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (34 points)
  • Panchayati Raj is a system of democratic decentralisation. Its objective is to bring the development to the grass-root level.
  • There are provisions related to Panchayati Raj in Part-IX from Article 243 to Article 243-O in the Indian-Constitution.
  • 16 New Articles in Part-IX and the 11th Schedule wear added in Indian Constitution by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act 1992. Total 29 subjects are mentioned in the 11th Schedule on which, the State legislature may, by law, endow the Panchayats with such powers and authority necessary to enable them to implement schemes for economic development and social justice.
  • Panchayati Raj is a subject of state list.
  • The state legislature determines provisions related to the structure of panchayats by law.
  • The State legislature makes decisions with respect to all matters relating to elections to the Panchayat. The State legislatures makes decision by law. The State Election Commission has superintendence, direction, control of rolls & conduct of elections.
  • It is conducted every 5 years.
  • There is a provision to form a Finance Commission to review the financial condition of panchayats.
  • Gram Sabha, is formed by the people registered in the electoral rolls of a village.
  • Article 40 of the Indian Constitution directs the state to organize village panchayats.
  • Balwant Rai Mehta committee recommended the establishment of a three-tier Panchayati Raj system at the Village level, Block level and District level.
  • Balwant Rai Mehta is called the Architect of the Panchayati Raj system.
  • The inauguration of Panchayati Raj system was done by Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru on 2nd October 1959 at Nagaur (Rajasthan).
  • Panchayati Raj institutions got constitutional status by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act.
  • Firstly the Laxmi Mal Singhvi Committee in 1986 and then P.K. Thungan Committee in 1988 recommended Panchayati Raj Institutions be given constitutional status.
  • Earlier, Ashok Mehta Committee, in 1977 proposed that some provisions of Panchayati Raj can be kept in the Indian Constitution, so the Government of India should think over it.
  • Due to the collapse of the Janta Government, no action could be taken on the recommendations of the Ashok Mehta Committee at the Central Level.
  • So, the recommendations of Laxmi Mal Singhvi and P.K. Thungan committee are clearly accepted. Major recommendations of the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee are also accepted in the Part IX of the Constitution.
  • According to Article 243-D(3) for seats and under Article 243D(4) for Chairperson's office, women are given 1/3rd reservation at all levels of Panchayats.
  • The minimum age to become a member of the Panchayat is 21 years.
  • The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act 1992, gives constitutional status to the Urban Local Self-government.
  • By this Amendment Act, a new part [Part IX A] and the 12th Schedule were added to the Constitution.
  • There are 8 types of local self-government which include Municipal Corporation, Municipality, Notified Area Committee, Town Area Committee, Cantonment Board, Township, Major Port Authority/Port Authority (earlier, Port Trust) and Special Purpose Agencies.
  • The 74thAmendmentAct provides three types of municipalities.
  • This includes Municipal Corporation, Municipal Council and a Nagar Panchayat.
  • All the members of the municipality are elected by the people of that area directly. [additional representation may be provided under Article 243R(2)].
  • The term of the municipality is 5 years, but it can be terminated earlier also.
  • The State Election Commission has the right to direct, control and manage the elections for the municipalities and Panchayats.
  • A Finance Commission is constituted under Article 243 I for municipalities and Panchayats.

The Financial Review is specified under Article 243 Y.

  • A District Planning committee is constituted under Article 243 ZD (1) at the District level to consolidate the plans prepared by the Municipalities and Panchayats in the district and to draft a development plan for the district as a whole.
  • According to Article 243ZE, in every metropolitan area, a metropolitan planning committee is to be constituted to prepare a draft development plan for the metropolitan area as a whole.
  • In India the first Municipal Corporation was established in Madras in the year 1688.
  • Lord Ripon is known as the father of local self-government in India.

Sir Charles Metcalfe (acting Governor General), 1830 → called Indian village communities 'little republics', nearly self-sufficient.

Chapter 42

Special Provisions Relating to Certain Classes

26 facts · 3 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (16 points)
  • The special provisions relating to certain classes are contained in Part XVI of the Constitution from Articles 330 to 342 A.
  • Part XVI also includes Articles 330A, 332A and 334A inserted by the Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023.
  • Article 330 provides for the reservation of seats for SCs and STs in the House of the People.
  • Under Article 331, provision was made for the representation of the Anglo-Indian community in the House of the people. It is noteworthy that the arrangements of nominating representatives of the Anglo Indian Community in the House of the People have also not been extended beyond the stipulated date (25 January, 2020) by 'the Constitution (One Hundred and Fourth Amendment) Act, 2019.
  • Article 332 provides for the reservation of seats for SCs and STs in the legislative assemblies of the States.
  • Under Article 333, provision was made for the representation of the Anglo-Indian Community in the Legislative Assemblies of the States. It is noteworthy that the arrangements of nominating representatives of the Anglo-Indian Community in the Legislative Assemblies of the states have also not been extended beyond the stipulated date (25 January, 2020) by 'the Constitution (One Hundred and Fourth Amendment) Act, 2019.
  • Article 338 provides for provisions relating to the National Commission for SCs.
  • At present, Kishor Makwana is the chairman of this commission.
  • Article 338A was added by the 89th Constitutional Amendment Act 2003, which provides for a separate National Commission for STs.
  • The President can appoint a commission to investigate the conditions of Socially and educationally backward classes (Article 340).
  • The President can declare any caste, race, tribe, part or groups of a State/U.T. as a Scheduled Caste after consulting with the Governor of that State. (Article 341(1)).
  • The President can declare any caste of a state/UT as a Scheduled Tribe after consulting with the Governor of that State [Article 342(1)]. Note: The Constitution (One Hundred and Fourth Amendment) Act, 2019 provides for extending the period of reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes for the next 10 years, whereas the provision for nomination of Anglo-Indian members has not been made beyond the predetermined date (25 January, 2020). So, currently this arrangement has ended. Newly added Articles in Part XVI (added by the 106th Constitution Amendment Act, 2023) have provisions as mentioned below.

Article 300 A: As nearly as may be, one-third (including the number of seats reserved for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes) of the total number of seats to be filled by direct election to the House of the People shall be reserved for women.

Article 332 A: As nearly as may be, one-third of the total number of seats to be filled by direct election to the Legislative Assembly of every State shall be reserved for women (including the number of seats reserved for women of SC and ST categories).

Article 334 A: When the Reservation of Seats for Women takes effect: The reservation, of one-third of the total seats to be filled by direct election, for women shall take effect after a delimitation is undertaken for the figures of the first Census taken after the commencement of the 106th Constitution Amendment Act, 2023.

This reservation shall cease to have effect, on the expiration of a period of fifteen years from such commencement.

Part XVI (Arts 330-342A) → special provisions for certain classes: Art 330 SC/ST seats in Lok Sabha; Art 331 Anglo-Indian representation in Lok Sabha.
